Article Title: California student Orion Greene, 16, spearheaded a seven-week blood cancer campaign in memory of his father; the team raised a record $1,234,579
Article Text:
For 16-year-old Orion Greene of San Rafael, Calif., his father's death became the impetus for a remarkable mission

A son’s tribute to his father

In his final months, John decided to forgo treatment and spend more time with his family

Transforming grief into hope

A family committed to the cause

It was not a single act of generosity, but a continuation of a legacy Orion has long been committed to.

Thousands of students and one mission

Building future leaders, changing lives

It is reported that thousands of students and volunteers participated in the 2026 campaign nationwide.

Some legacies are counted in wealth or in achievement. Others are motivated by compassion, resilience and a determination to ensure no other family ever experiences the same heartbreak. For 16-year-old Orion Greene of San Rafael, Calif., his father's death became the impetus for a remarkable mission. In a record-shattering fundraising effort, the high school student rallied classmates, volunteers, family members and supporters over seven weeks, raising $1,234,579 to support blood cancer research, patient support and advocacy. His work has now won him the title of 2026 National Student Visionary of the Year from Blood Cancer Unit, states Blood Cancer United's official report. The news report states that the campaign was a fundraising challenge and became a tribute to a father who had fought blood cancer for years and spent much of his life helping others who fought the same disease.Orion is a student at San Rafael High School and started the campaign in memory of his father, John Greene, who was with Blood Cancer United for many years. In the past 15 years, John has had acute myeloid leukemia (AML) several times.He had three stem cell transplants during that time, but continued to fight for blood cancer awareness and fundraising. He previously served on the organization’s board, raising more than $8 million to support patients, scientific research and advocacy initiatives. In his final months, John decided to forgo treatment and spend more time with his family. Instead of walking away from the cause, he stayed involved and helped Orion develop what would become the most successful Student Visionaries of the Year campaign in the program’s history.Orion didn’t allow personal loss to define the campaign, instead, he turned it into a movement that invited an entire community to contribute. The report states that during the seven-week campaign, the team – called the “Greene Goblins” – worked together on creative fundraising projects, along with other students. And one of the coolest things the campaign did was put together a custom merchandise collection based on two things John loved: playing the piano and the family’s cat, Katniss. Merchandise created by Orion’s mother, Heather Greene, was sold online and at John’s Celebration of Life, allowing friends and supporters to honor his memory while supporting the cause. It is reported that John was a respected employee at Salesforce and the campaign benefited greatly from Salesforce. In his honor, the family’s memorial gathering was enhanced by a generous contribution from the company.The Greene family’s connection to Blood Cancer United didn't start with Orion's campaign. Over the years, they have participated in community walks, local fundraising events and even childhood bake sales to help support blood cancer patients. Orion’s older brother, Floyd Greene, had also been a member of the Student Visionaries of the Year program, continuing a family tradition of giving back. It was not a single act of generosity, but a continuation of a legacy Orion has long been committed to.For the uninitiated, Student Visionaries of the Year is one of Blood Cancer United’s signature leadership programs, inspiring high school students across the United States to learn fundraising, entrepreneurship, marketing and project management skills while supporting blood cancer research and patient care. It is reported that thousands of students and volunteers participated in the 2026 campaign nationwide and while the Orion team won the top national honor, a number of other teams also had extraordinary results. Team BE-VALuable for a Cure, led by Isabella Nilio and Valentina DePaço from Villa Walsh Academy in New Jersey, raised $715,271 and finished as national runners-up. A second New Jersey team, "BC We Care," co-led by Darian Petillo and Valentina Reale, raised over $700,000 to finish a close second. Meanwhile, eighth-grader Gray Shields was named National Team Member of the Year after raising $210,122 on his own.Beyond the impressive fundraising figures, the Student Visionaries of the Year program is designed to nurture leadership in young people, giving them hands-on experience in organising campaigns, engaging communities and tackling complex challenges. Participants make a difference for families affected by blood cancers such as leukemia, lymphoma and myeloma, while gaining real-world skills that extend well beyond fundraising. Sunbelt Rentals, the National Presenting Partner for the 2026 campaign season, also supported the effort to grow community participation across the country. This campaign reminds us that in the face of profound loss, one person’s determination can inspire an entire community to unite—transforming grief into hope and opening the door for better treatments and brighter futures for families impacted by blood cancer.Images Courtesy: Blood Cancer United Website
Article Summary: Orion Greene of San Rafael, Calif., raised $1,234,579 to support blood cancer research, patient support and advocacy. His work has now won him the title of 2026 National Student Visionary of the Year from Blood Cancer Unit. The campaign was a fundraising challenge and became a tribute to a father who had fought blood cancer for years.

Article Title: Scientists created the world's whitest paint that reflects 98.1% of sunlight and it could cool buildings without air conditioning
Article Text:
PC: Purdue University

How the world's whitest paint reduces heat build-up

What makes the world's whitest paint so white

How this cooling paint lowers surface temperatures

Years of experimentation behind a simple-looking finish

More than laboratory research

A possible role in reducing building energy demand

Keeping buildings cool has become an increasingly difficult challenge as temperatures rise and air conditioning demand continues to grow. While cooling systems provide comfort, they also consume large amounts of electricity, adding to energy costs and greenhouse gas emissions. That has encouraged scientists to look for alternatives that work with nature rather than against it. One promising approach is to prevent buildings from heating up in the first place by reflecting as much sunlight as possible.A team of engineers at Purdue University believes it has taken a significant step in that direction after developing an exceptionally reflective white paint designed to cool surfaces naturally, even under direct sunlight.The new coating was created to bounce away nearly all of the Sun's incoming energy instead of allowing it to be absorbed by roofs and walls. Reportedly, laboratory measurements showed that the paint reflects around 98.1% of sunlight, placing it beyond the performance of conventional white exterior paints and even ahead of the team's earlier experimental version.That difference may appear small at first glance, but when spread across the roof of a building exposed to strong sunlight throughout the day, the improvement becomes meaningful.Standard white paints usually absorb enough solar energy that they still warm up. Even specialist "cool roof" products generally reflect between 80 and 90% of sunlight, meaning surfaces remain warmer than the surrounding air.The research published in the journal ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces, titled ‘ Ultrawhite BaSO4 Paints and Films for Remarkable Daytime Subambient Radiative Cooling ’ where the team described the paint as one of the highest-performing single-layer radiative cooling coatings developed so far. By combining exceptionally high solar reflectance with strong infrared emission in a paint that can be applied using familiar methods, the work offers a practical example of how materials engineering could help buildings stay cooler using less energy.Achieving such a high level of reflectivity required more than simply adding extra white pigment.The research team selected barium sulfate as the primary material after comparing a wide range of naturally white substances. The compound is already familiar in everyday products, including cosmetics and photographic paper, because of its bright appearance. Its optical properties also make it highly effective at scattering sunlight.Equally important was the size of the particles inside the paint. Rather than using particles of a uniform diameter, the engineers deliberately mixed many different sizes together. Since each particle interacts with different wavelengths of sunlight, combining a broad range allows more of the solar spectrum to be reflected back into the environment instead of being absorbed by the painted surface. Packing too many particles into the mixture could make the paint more likely to crack or peel once applied, so the researchers balanced reflectivity with long-term durability.Outdoor testing showed that the paint could lower surface temperatures beyond what passive shade or conventional coatings normally achieve.During daytime measurements under strong sunshine, coated samples stayed roughly 4.5°C below the surrounding air temperature. After sunset, when radiative cooling became even more effective, surfaces were measured at around 10.5°C cooler than the ambient air.The effect was also observed during colder weather. In one winter test, despite air temperatures of approximately 6°C, the painted sample still maintained a considerably lower surface temperature.According to the researchers, covering a roof area of roughly 1,000 square feet with the coating could provide a cooling effect equivalent to about 10 kilowatts under favourable conditions. That figure exceeds the cooling capacity of many residential central air conditioning systems, although real-world performance would depend on local climate, roof design and weather conditions.Although the finished product resembles ordinary white paint, reaching this point took years of trial and error.The Purdue group spent around six years investigating materials suitable for passive radiative cooling. More than 100 candidate substances were considered before narrowing the list to a handful worthy of detailed testing. Each promising material went through dozens of formulation changes as the team searched for the right balance between optical performance, reliability and ease of manufacture.An earlier version of the project relied on calcium carbonate, a material commonly found in rocks and seashells. That paint already demonstrated strong cooling performance, but switching to barium sulfate allowed the researchers to improve sunlight reflection even further without abandoning a manufacturing process that remains compatible with commercial paint production.The work was intended with practical use in mind rather than remaining a purely academic exercise.The team says the formulation can be produced using techniques already familiar to the paint industry, making future commercial development more realistic. Tests also suggested that the coating can withstand outdoor exposure in a way comparable with existing architectural paints.Patent applications covering the formulation have been submitted through Purdue University's technology commercialisation office. The research itself was supported by the Cooling Technologies Research Center at Purdue University and the US Air Force Office of Scientific Research.Passive cooling has attracted growing attention because it reduces heat without consuming electricity. Instead of relying on compressors, refrigerants or powered ventilation, radiative cooling materials allow buildings to shed heat naturally while reflecting incoming solar radiation.If coatings like Purdue's can be produced at scale and remain durable over many years, they could reduce cooling demand for homes, offices, warehouses and industrial buildings in warm climates. They are unlikely to replace air conditioning entirely in every setting, particularly during periods of extreme heat or high humidity, but they could reduce the amount of mechanical cooling needed.
Article Summary: Engineers at Purdue University have developed an exceptionally reflective white paint designed to cool surfaces naturally, even under direct sunlight. The new coating was created to bounce away nearly all of the Sun's incoming energy instead of allowing it to be absorbed by roofs and walls. Standard white paints usually absorb enough solar energy that they still warm up.

Article Title: Pakistan crackdown in PoK draws protests on UK streets
Article Text:
Bradford, UK (ANI photo)

Unrest continues in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) as a crackdown by Pakistani authorities has triggered growing anger among residents. On Wednesday, members of the British Kashmiri diaspora held a protest in UK's Bradford, expressing solidarity with the people of PoJK and backing the demands of the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC).The protest came as Pakistan-occupied Kashmir is in the middle of its so-called assembly elections, while Islamabad has intensified security operations in the region.Protesters gathered in Bradford city centre carrying banners and placards, demanding the protection of fundamental rights, civil liberties and human dignity. Organisers said the rally aimed to draw international attention as the worsening human rights situation in PoJK.Speakers at the protest claimed that security operations over the past two months had led to civilian deaths, created fear among residents and disrupted daily life. They also alleged that women, children and elderly people were among those affected.The protesters called for transparent and impartial investigations into allegations of excessive use of force, house raids and other reported human rights violations.They urged the authorities to ensure accountability and uphold the rule of law.They also appealed to the international community, human rights organisations and the British government to closely monitor the situation in PoJK and support efforts to protect fundamental freedoms and promote a peaceful resolution to the issues raised by local communities.According to the organisers, residents of PoJK have continued to face action by Pakistani security forces, with several people reportedly killed or injured during firing on protesters in recent months. They also alleged that the ongoing elections in the region have seen low voter turnout and irregularities.The protesters said that people in PoJK are demanding an end to Pakistan's control over the territory and are urging the international community to play a greater role in restoring peace, ensuring accountability and safeguarding the lives and rights of the local population.Meanwhile, India has also strongly condemned the neighbouring Pakistan's crackdown on PoK. The ministry of external affairs called the local elections as "a complete farce."The MEA also highlighted the situation gripped with violence, blackouts, intimidation, and repression against civilians.
Article Summary: Members of the British Kashmiri diaspora held a protest in UK's Bradford, expressing solidarity with the people of PoJK. The protest came as Pakistan- occupied Kashmir is in the middle of its so-called assembly elections. Islamabad has intensified security operations in the region.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Jackie Chan: "I never wanted to be the next Bruce Lee. I just wanted to be…" - an inspiring lesson on finding your own path
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Jackie Chan (AP photo)

Quote of the day by Jackie Chan

"I never wanted to be the next Bruce Lee . I just wanted to be the first Jackie Chan"

What is the meaning behind Jackie Chan’s quote

The real story behind this quote by Jackie Chan

Why individuality creates lasting success

Why role models should inspire rather than define someone

Why confidence tends to grow from authenticity

Why choosing a different path takes real courage

Why this idea reaches well beyond entertainment

Other famous quotes by Jackie Chan

"I want to be an Asian Robert De Niro."

"The life of an action star is very short. I want to be an actor like Robert De Niro, like Dustin Hoffman or Clint Eastwood who in their 70s or 80s can still act."

"We learn martial arts as helping weakness. You never fight for people to get hurt. You're always helping people."

"I started my Jackie Chan Foundation to help children and sick kids and people in hospitals."

Why Jackie Chan's message continues to inspire

Every generation looks up to role models. Students admire great teachers, athletes dream of becoming sporting legends, and young professionals often aspire to follow the paths of industry leaders. While inspiration is genuinely valuable, constantly trying to become someone else can prevent people from ever discovering their own unique strengths, a lesson Jackie Chan learned directly while stepping out from under the shadow of the biggest star his industry had ever produced. His own path from working stuntman to global icon shows exactly what that lesson looks like when it is actually lived out, rather than simply repeated as advice.Jackie Chan is expressing the value of authenticity. Rather than trying to replace Bruce Lee or copy his achievements, Chan focused on building his own identity instead. The quote teaches that inspiration should never quietly turn into imitation. Learning from successful people is genuinely valuable, but lasting achievement tends to come from building on your own personality, talents and experiences. True success gets measured by becoming the best version of yourself, not by becoming a convincing copy of someone else.After Bruce Lee's death in 1973, film producers searched for someone who could carry his legacy forward, and Chan, who had actually worked as a young stuntman on Lee's own films, was pushed to become his successor. He has described their very first meeting directly. Working as a stuntman earning around eighty cents a day, Chan was accidentally hit by Lee during a staged fight scene, and rather than letting the moment pass, he played up the injury to get some sympathy. "I wanted him to hit me again," Chan later joked, recalling how attentive Lee became afterward.Once producers began grooming him as Lee's replacement, Chan made a deliberate decision to go in the opposite direction entirely. "I said: I am not Bruce Lee," he explained. "So, if Bruce kicked high, I kick low. Bruce fights like this. I do it the opposite. That's Jackie Chan. I just do myself." He combined martial arts with genuine comedy, performed his own dangerous stunts, and developed a screen presence built on vulnerability and humour rather than raw intensity, eventually becoming one of the most recognisable action stars in the world.People often compare themselves with those who came before them. While comparison can occasionally provide motivation, it can just as easily limit creativity. Chan became successful specifically because he introduced something genuinely different to action cinema. His humour, physical comedy and inventive stunt work created a style audiences had never quite seen before. Originality, in his case, became his single greatest strength.Role models offer valuable lessons, demonstrating discipline, determination and real excellence. Even so, every person's journey is different, and trying to copy someone else's path exactly can quietly stop people recognising their own actual opportunities. Chan has said he learned an enormous amount from watching Bruce Lee's films, even turning to them during difficult periods. Learning from someone and becoming their replacement were never really the same thing.Pretending to be someone else takes constant, exhausting effort. Being authentic lets confidence develop far more naturally instead. People who genuinely embrace their own strengths tend to communicate more effectively, make clearer decisions, and build stronger relationships along the way. Authenticity tends to attract trust precisely because it reflects honesty rather than performance.Choosing originality is rarely easy. New ideas often face real scepticism before they gain any acceptance. Chan's blend of martial arts and comedy differed sharply from the serious action heroes audiences were used to at the time, and his early attempts in Hollywood were not immediately successful either. His willingness to keep taking creative risks eventually turned him into a genuine international star.Chan's message extends far beyond films, applying just as directly to students choosing careers, entrepreneurs building businesses, artists developing their own style, athletes competing at the highest level, and professionals stepping into leadership roles. Everyone benefits from recognising that originality tends to create far greater long-term success than imitation ever could.Chan's words are a reminder that the greatest achievements often come from embracing who you genuinely are rather than trying to become someone else. Every person carries a unique story, a unique perspective and a unique set of strengths. "I never wanted to be the next Bruce Lee. I just wanted to be the first Jackie Chan" is really more than a reflection on one actor's own career. It is a philosophy of authenticity, teaching that inspiration should guide people rather than define them, and that true success comes from building a legacy that genuinely reflects your own identity rather than living permanently in someone else's shadow. That is why his message continues to resonate across generations, since the most memorable people are rarely those who perfectly imitate greatness, but those with the courage to become unmistakably themselves.
Article Summary: Jackie Chan is expressing the value of authenticity. Rather than trying to replace Bruce Lee or copy his achievements, Chan focused on building his own identity. The quote teaches that inspiration should never quietly turn into imitation. True success gets measured by becoming the best version of yourself, not by becoming a convincing copy of someone else.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Jackie Chan: 'You don't get to do over parts or go back and change your path. Your life is decided by...' and how split-second choices reveal who you really are when there's no saf
Article Text:
Jackie Chan is a Hong Kong actor, filmmaker, and martial artist known worldwide for performing his own dangerous stunts and blending action with comedy

Project A

Never Grow Up

"You don't get to do over parts or go back and change your path.

Your life is decided by your character and the decisions you make in the moment."

From the China drama academy to international fame

Fist of Fury

Enter the Dragon

Never Grow Up

Armour of God

Rumble in the Bronx

The philosophy of actions that cannot be repeated

Nicomachean Ethics

The lasting impact of high-stakes decisions

While filming the 1983 martial arts comedy, a stunt performer stood at the edge of a clock tower, looking down at a drop of more than 15 metres. Below him were only thin canvas awnings meant to soften the fall. The man was Jackie Chan . He made the jump, crashed through the awnings, landed on his neck, and seriously injured his cervical spine.He survived, recovered, and later performed the stunt again to get the exact shot he wanted. There were no digital safety wires to remove later, no chance to change his path while falling, and no computer-generated effects to protect him.Years later, in his 2018 memoir(co-written with Zhu Mo and translated into English by Thorsten Boose), Chan reflected on a career built around real physical danger:His words challenge the idea that life offers endless second chances. Modern culture often focuses on looking back, rewriting stories, or editing mistakes. Real life does not work that way. The choices people make under pressure, shaped by their habits and values, become a permanent part of their lives.Jackie Chan's outlook was shaped by an environment where mistakes had immediate physical consequences.Born Chan Kong-sang in Hong Kong in 1954, he entered the China Drama Academy at the age of seven. The school, run by Master Yu Jim-yuen, trained children in Peking Opera through a strict and demanding routine.For ten years, Chan spent up to 19 hours a day practising acrobatics, martial arts, and stage performance. Discipline was strict, and corporal punishment was common.Getting a stunt or flip wrong often resulted in immediate physical pain. There was little room for hesitation, mistakes, or excuses.When Chan joined Hong Kong's film industry as a stuntman in the early 1970s, working on Bruce Lee films such as(1972) and(1973), action movies relied heavily on real stunts. Stunt performers earned modest pay while taking serious physical risks.By the time Chan publishedin 2018 at the age of 64, his body carried lasting reminders of that career. He had a plastic plate in his skull after a near-fatal fall during the filming of(1986), a badly broken ankle from(1995), and many other broken bones.Rather than celebrating only his success, the memoir offers an honest and often self-critical look at his personal mistakes, weaknesses, and career decisions. Chan explains that while a film director can shout "cut" and restart a scene, people must live with every decision they make.Chan's message reflects ideas that have existed in philosophy for thousands of years.The ancient Greek philosopher Heraclitus expressed a similar idea when he said that "no man ever steps in the same river twice, for it's not the same river and he's not the same man." Time only moves forward, and no moment can ever be repeated exactly.The second part of Chan's quote connects quick decisions with personal character. This idea lies at the heart of Aristotle's virtue ethics. In the, Aristotle argued that good character is not something people simply think about. Instead, it is built through repeated actions and habits over time.When people face a crisis, they do not have time to create a new moral code. Instead, they react according to the habits and values they have already developed.Whether on a movie set, a battlefield, or inside an emergency room, fast decisions usually reflect years of experience and deeply formed character.Modern behavioural economics supports this view. Psychologist Daniel Kahneman's dual-process theory describes two ways of thinking: System 1, which is fast and instinctive, and System 2, which is slower and more deliberate.During emergencies, there is often no time for careful analysis. People rely mainly on System 1, which draws on long-practised habits, experience, and patterns built through years of everyday decisions.Modern life often creates the illusion that everything can be fixed. Computer software can be updated, digital photos can be edited, and social media posts can be deleted within minutes.But in many important areas of life, time moves only in one direction.In business leadership, moments of crisis show how much immediate decisions matter. During the 1982 Tylenol poisoning crisis, Johnson & Johnson CEO James Burke quickly decided to recall 31 million bottles of medicine, even though it cost the company more than $100 million.His decision followed the company's long-standing belief that public safety should come before profits. That choice helped protect the company's reputation, while leaders who delay or try to hide problems often cause lasting damage to their organisations.The same principle applies in aviation. National Transportation Safety Board investigations show that many emergency outcomes are decided within seconds. When Captain Chesley Sullenberger safely landed US Airways Flight 1549 on the Hudson River in 2009 after both engines failed following bird strikes, he had less than three minutes to make a decision.The successful landing was not simply good luck. It was the result of four decades of flying experience, disciplined training, and calm judgment applied during a situation that allowed no second chance.Living without a rewind button means accepting that every decision leaves a permanent mark. Although past mistakes cannot be undone, the character people bring to the next important moment remains fully within their control.
Article Summary: Jackie Chan is a Hong Kong actor, filmmaker, and martial artist. He is known worldwide for performing his own dangerous stunts and blending action with comedy. In his 2018 memoir, Chan reflected on a career built around real physical danger. His words challenge the idea that life offers endless second chances.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Carl Weathers: "I majored in theater at San Diego State. My one eye was on football, and my other eye was on…"
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Carl Weathers (AP photo)

Quote of the day by Carl Weathers

"I majored in theater at San Diego State. My one eye was on football, and my other eye was on Hollywood"

Where this quote actually comes from, and what it genuinely meant

What the quote still teaches, honestly told

The real story behind his own path into football

Why real setbacks can end up redirecting someone toward something better

Why staying versatile still matters, even when it costs something

Why ambition never really needs to stay narrow

Why this idea reaches well beyond football and Hollywood

A note on Carl Weathers' journey

Other memorable quotes by Carl Weathers

"My first love was acting. I went to Sidney Poitier films as a kid. I sat in the theater and dreamed of being an actor."

"I really try to take care of myself. I really put forth the effort to make a regimen just a part of my life."

Why this timeless message still resonates

People often get told to pick one path and pour everything into it, whether in sport, education or career. Carl Weathers , later known worldwide for playing Apollo Creed in the Rocky films, described a life that never really worked that way. "I majored in theater at San Diego State," he said. "My one eye was on football, and my other eye was on Hollywood. " He was pursuing two very different ambitions at once, and honest enough later to admit that split focus came with a real cost, one that ultimately shaped how his entire career actually unfolded.Weathers said this in a 2007 interview with Sporting News, and the fuller quote reveals something more candid than it first appears. "I'll give you a completely honest answer. I wasn't present," he said. "I was a guy who had a tremendous amount of ability, but my head was always in the world of wanting to be an actor. I majored in theater at San Diego State. My one eye was on football, and my other eye was on Hollywood." This was not a celebration of successfully juggling two dreams at once. It was Weathers explaining, honestly, why his football career never fully lived up to his actual ability, because part of his attention was always somewhere else.Even framed this way, the quote still carries real value. Weathers is not pretending divided attention comes free of cost. He is showing that a passion pursued alongside something else can still end up mattering more in the long run, even if it means the original path never reaches its full potential. His football career fell short of what his raw ability suggested was possible. His acting career, built on the same drive that had quietly pulled his focus away from football, went on to define the rest of his life.Weathers began his football career at Long Beach City College in 1966 as a freshman defensive end, before an ankle injury during practice cut that stint short. He transferred to San Diego State University, playing defensive end under Don Coryell, a coach later inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame. He went on to a brief professional career, including time with the Oakland Raiders, before turning fully toward acting. Notably, he never actually boxed before playing Apollo Creed. The physique that made him convincing in the role came entirely from his years playing football, not from any boxing training at all.Not every plan works out the way it was originally intended. Weathers' own professional football career was genuinely short, and by his own account, not what his ability should have produced. Rather than treating that as pure failure, he simply kept pursuing acting with the same determination, and that redirected path ended up defining the rest of his career far beyond what football alone might have offered.Modern careers rarely run in a single straight line. People change professions, pick up new skills, and adapt to entirely different industries more often than earlier generations typically did. Being versatile tends to build real resilience, even when, as in Weathers' own case, it means one particular pursuit never gets the singular focus it might have needed to fully succeed.Society often nudges people toward defining themselves through one single role. Weathers' own life shows that identity can genuinely be broader than that, an athlete and an actor, someone whose background in one field ended up directly shaping his success in a completely different one.Although Weathers was speaking specifically about his own two pursuits, the underlying lesson applies more broadly. A student weighing different career paths. A professional considering an unrelated qualification. Anyone genuinely balancing more than one interest. Divided focus has a real cost, as Weathers himself openly admitted, but it can still lead somewhere worth reaching.Carl Weathers, who lived from 1948 to 2024, began his career as a college and briefly professional American football player before becoming an acclaimed actor, director and producer. He gained worldwide recognition as Apollo Creed in the Rocky film series, and later appeared in films including Predator and Happy Gilmore, along with television roles in Arrested Development and The Mandalorian. He died on 1 February 2024, at the age of 76.Weathers' words are a reminder that people do not always have to choose cleanly between competing passions, even though pursuing more than one rarely comes without genuine cost. Skills built in one pursuit can end up becoming the actual foundation for success somewhere else entirely. His own honesty about not being fully present in his football career, paired with where that same divided attention eventually led him, is really the whole lesson in miniature. Life rarely follows a single script, and sometimes the path that looks like a distraction turns out to be exactly where the real opportunity was waiting.
Article Summary: Carl Weathers is known worldwide for playing Apollo Creed in the Rocky films. Weathers began his football career at Long Beach City College in 1966. He went on to a brief professional career, including time with the Oakland Raiders. He later became an acclaimed actor, director and producer.

Article Title: NOC to travel outside Islamabad, Lahore, Karachi - Pakistan restricts foreign journalists amid PoK crackdown
Article Text:
Pakistan tightens curbs on foreign media (Reuters image)

Pakistan has imposed fresh restrictions on foreign media personnel, requiring journalists working for international news organisations to obtain a No Objection Certificate (NOC) before travelling outside Islamabad, Lahore and Karachi for reporting assignments.The new guidelines, issued by Pakistan's ministry of information and broadcasting (MoIB), establish a comprehensive framework governing the registration, accreditation and movement of foreign media organisations and journalists operating in the country.Under the rules, journalists are exempt from the No Objection Certificate (NOC) requirement when travelling within Islamabad, Lahore and Karachi. For personal travel to Abbottabad and Murree, they may apply for an NOC through the ministry's External Publicity (EP) Wing, with approvals expected within three working days.“All Pakistani journalists residing abroad, contributing to foreign media and seeking registration must submit their application through the EP Wing portal and concurrently forward their case through the nearest press attaché, counsellor, minister posted in Pakistan missions, consulates, high commissions, or embassies,” the MOIB said, as cited by Dawn.Additionally, the guidelines require all companies, entities, production houses and other organisations operating in Pakistan to facilitate foreign media "in any capacity" to register with the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting's publicity wing.The registration requirement also applies to non-journalists residing in Pakistan who provide services to foreign media organisations.The new rules apply to all international media organisations, including print, electronic and digital outlets, as well as web-based platforms and social media organisations.The regulations also require production houses, companies, freelancers, fixers and non-journalists providing services to foreign media in Pakistan to register with the ministry. It clarified that the registration is intended solely for professional recognition and does not grant any official status."All foreign/international media personnel already accredited or registered with EP Wing shall be required a mandatory NOC from EP Wing for movement to any other city (except Islamabad, Lahore and Karachi) in case they are going to produce a news content, story, video, film, documentary or social media content for their official use," the guidelines state.After completing the registration process, journalists seeking a press accreditation card must submit an application through the online portal along with the required documents. The guidelines provide for two categories of accreditation: permanent accreditation, issued annually, and temporary accreditation for visiting journalists, valid for up to three months.Once the external publicity wing issues the accreditation card, it will "facilitate" journalists' access to official media events and government premises.The guidelines state that journalists will be "bound to produce that card on demand", and must surrender it if they change their organisation or accreditation category, or when the accreditation period expires.The latest measures come amid heightened scrutiny of media access in Pakistan following reports of protests, disruptions and the alleged use of force during the local election process in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK).Human rights and press freedom organisations, including Amnesty International and Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), have raised concerns over alleged restrictions on journalists, communication blackouts, enforced disappearances of media personnel and curbs on foreign media coverage of the protests. Amnesty International has also called for an independent investigation into allegations of excessive force used against demonstrators in Rawalakot.
Article Summary: New guidelines establish framework governing registration, accreditation and movement of foreign media. Journalists exempt from NOC requirement when travelling within Islamabad, Lahore and Karachi. For personal travel to Abbottabad and Murree, they may apply for NOC through ministry's External Publicity (EP) Wing.

Article Title: Russian drone chases Ukrainian vegetable seller in 'safari' attack - Watch
Article Text:
Russian drone targets Ukrainian vegetable seller in 'Safari' attack

Ukraine on Tuesday accused Russia of committing a war crime after footage emerged showing a Russian drone pursuing and striking a vegetable seller in the southern city of Kherson, leaving the civilian wounded.Video footage shows a drone pursuing a man around a van being used as a roadside vegetable stall before exploding as he dives behind the vehicle for cover. Police said the man, in his 50s, survived the attack but sustained shrapnel injuries and suffered shock.Reacting to the incident, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the latest footage highlighted what he described as Russia's continued targeting of civilians in Kherson."Today, many were shocked by yet another video of the drone 'safari' Russians are carrying out against civilians in Kherson," Zelenskyy said in a post on X, adding that "Russia has gone mad" and calling for increased pressure on Moscow and strong security guarantees for Ukraine."The world must see this. It must see every piece of evidence that Russia has gone mad and that its soldiers take pleasure in killing and abusing civilians.Without pressure on Russia, the dismantling of its capacity for aggression, and real security guarantees, it is simply impossible to imagine the world being able to coexist with this evil. We must remain resolute in defending life. We must act and support life in ways that force Russia to seriously think about peace rather than expanding the range of its drones," Zelenskyy added.Ukrainian authorities later identified the victim only as 52-year-old Yurii and released a video interview with him from the hospital.According to Oleksandr Prokudin head of the Kherson regional military administration, Yurii had travelled to Kherson that morning to sell vegetables. Prokudin shared the hospital interview on Telegram.Yurii said he and his wife were arranging crates of vegetables beside their van when he heard the distinctive buzz of a drone overhead. As his wife fled, he said, the drone turned its attention to him. He recalled holding up several heads of garlic toward the drone's camera to signal to its operator that he was not filming it."It could see that I had tomatoes out, some cucumbers and eggplants laid out on the floor," Yurii said, as cited by the BBC. "It even ducked under the umbrella when I was running away round the other side."So-called "safari" attacks, in which drones are allegedly used to hunt civilians, have been reported in Kherson for months. The southern city lies just a few miles from the front line.A 2025 United Nations report said it found that Russian armed forces had "recurrently killed and injured civilians" in the area by using drones to target them.Ukraine has also carried out drone and long-range missile strikes inside Russia, which Russian authorities say have resulted in civilian casualties.Russia on Monday accused Ukraine of carrying out a "terrorist" attack after seven people, including three children, were killed at the Black Sea resort town of Gelendzhik in what Moscow described as a deliberate drone strike targeting civilians.
Article Summary: Video footage shows a drone pursuing a man around a van being used as a roadside vegetable stall. Police said the man, in his 50s, survived the attack but sustained shrapnel injuries and suffered shock. Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the latest footage highlighted what he described as Russia's continued targeting of civilians.

Article Title: 'We'll know in 48 hours': Trump warns Iran to open Hormuz or get 'hit very hard'
Article Text:
US, Iran and Oman near interim deal to reopen Strait of Hormuz. Trump warns Tehran to reach a deal soon.

US president Donald Trump has signalled that a possible breakthrough in talks with Iran could come within 48 hours, while warning Tehran that the Strait of Hormuz must reopen “very soon” as part of a deal with Iran and Oman, or face military action.Speaking to reporters in California on Tuesday, Trump said negotiations with Iran were “moving along very nicely”. “We’ll find out. We’ll know in 48 hours,” he added.The comments came as Axios reported that the US, Iran and Oman were nearing an interim agreement aimed at reopening the Strait of Hormuz, with Washington hoping for an announcement on Wednesday.The remarks came after Trump told Fox News that the two sides had held an “all-day negotiation”. The US president described the discussions positively while warning Iran could be hit “really hard” if a deal was not reached.“They had an all-day negotiation,” Trump told Fox News, adding, “We are having very good discussions."In an interview with Fox News, Trump linked the negotiations directly to the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.“The strait is going to be open very soon, or they’re going to get hit very hard – and then the strait’s going to be open,” Trump said.Trump also said Washington and Tehran were engaged in “very good discussions”, despite repeated Iranian denials of direct talks. “They don’t like to admit that, but yeah, it’s a little bit disconcerting,” he said.“The only thing that matters is action, and they want to make a deal. We’ll see what happens. If they don’t make a deal, it’s going to be too bad,” he added.Trump also reiterated that Iran would never have a nuclear weapon. "They already can't, but they'll--it's going to be formal. The strait's going to be open very soon, or they're going to get hit very hard, and then the strait's going to be open", he added.Trump said Washington had been preparing a major military operation against Iran before diplomacy took precedence after Tehran sought talks.“We were going into a tremendous attack, the biggest since World War II, and they called me and said, very politely, 'Please, can we talk? Can we talk?'” Trump told Fox News. “Yes, we can talk. Let's get it done.”Trump on Saturday postponed large-scale strikes against Iran after consultations with Gulf partners, giving diplomatic efforts more time.
Article Summary: US, Iran and Oman near interim deal to reopen Strait of Hormuz. Trump warns Tehran to reach a deal soon. Comments came as Axios reported that the US, Iran. and Oman were nearing an interim agreement aimed at reopening the Strait of. Hormuez.

Article Title: Seven blasts rock Dubai's Jebel Ali as massive fire erupts near strategic port amid Iran war
Article Text:
Multiple explosions rock Dubai's Jebel Ali

At least seven explosions were reported in Dubai's Jebel Ali industrial area early Wednesday, followed by a major fire along the United Arab Emirates coast, according to Iranian broadcaster Press TV.Iraqi media outlets reported that the explosions were caused by a missile attack launched from Yemen, while Emirati media, without citing an official statement, confirmed hearing multiple blasts. Nasa thermal imagery later indicated a fire at a warehouse near the port that is used for fuel storage and transfer, as cited by the Mehr news agency.Press TV also cited media reports claiming that UAE authorities had arrested two people for filming the fire after smoke was seen billowing from the site.Located in southwestern Dubai, Jebel Ali serves as one of the UAE's key logistics, commercial and industrial hubs. The area includes Jebel Ali Port and the Jebel Ali Free Zone (Jafza), established in 1985, which is home to more than 11,000 companies from over 150 countries. With links to major highways, Jebel Ali Port and Al Maktoum International Airport, the complex is a major gateway for international trade, according to Press TV.The development comes as US president Donald Trump said on Tuesday (local time) that the Strait of Hormuz would reopen "very soon" as part of an agreement involving Iran and Oman. He also warned that Iran would be "hit really hard" if it failed to reach a deal during ongoing talks aimed at easing regional tensions.Trump reiterated that Iran would not be allowed to acquire a nuclear weapon and said the reopening of the strategic waterway was tied to the broader diplomatic negotiations."Iran, as an example, will never have a nuclear weapon. They already can't, but they'll--it's going to be formal. The strait's going to be open very soon, or they're going to get hit very hard, and then the strait's going to be open," Trump said in an interview with Fox News.Trump's remarks came as the United States, Iran and Oman were reportedly nearing an interim agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, following heightened tensions after the collapse of a 14-point Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between Washington and Tehran last month, Axios reported, citing two regional sources and a US official.
Article Summary: At least seven explosions reported in Dubai's Jebel Ali industrial area, followed by a major fire. Iraqi media outlets reported that the explosions were caused by a missile attack launched from Yemen. Nasa thermal imagery later indicated a fire at a warehouse near the port that is used for fuel storage and transfer.

Article Title: Russia-Ukraine war intensifies: Overnight airstrikes kill 14 in Kyiv, damage warehouses, spark fire - watch
Article Text:
Footage of the explosion caused by the airstrikes (Photo: X/ @AMK_Mapping)​

Russian airstrikes on the Ukrainian capital Kyiv killed 14 early on Wednesday morning amid increased attacks on the capital. 27 others were injured as buildings and warehouses got damaged in a massive fire triggered by the strikes. The capital city of Ukraine experienced air raid alerts for over an hour and seven military sites were struck in an assault that began after midnight.Mayor Vitali Klitschko informed that one warehouse building had been destroyed near the city centre and rescue teams had pulled two people from the ruins.“There may still be people under the rubble”, he wrote on Telegram, adding that search and rescue operations are proceeding, with an ambulance driver being among the injured.Additionally, the city’s military administration said the assault caused an ammonia leak, which was being tackled by emergency crews.According to AFP, journalists heard explosions in Kyiv after midnight following a warning from the Ukrainian air force about incoming ballistic missiles.Kyiv’s military administration said the barrage damaged residential buildings and several warehouses.Earlier, Russian attacks on Saturday had killed 10 people and injured more than 30, while Ukrainian drones sank a large Russian container ship in the Black Sea.As Russia increases its use of ballistic missiles, Ukraine has urged its allies to provide more US-made Patriot interceptors.Both sides have stepped up long-range attacks in recent weeks. Russia more than doubled its use of missiles in July, according to an AFP analysis.Drone attacks have also become a regular occurrence, with Ukraine intensifying strikes on civilian infrastructure, including oil and gas facilities and logistics sites in Russia.On Tuesday morning, five people were killed, and 10 others were injured in the Moscow region as Ukraine targeted depots belonging to Russian e-commerce giant Wildberries, AFP reported.Moscow’s mayor said on Wednesday that Russian air defences had intercepted and destroyed at least 10 drones heading towards the capital.Meanwhile, Ukraine expressed outrage over a video showing a man being chased by a drone in the battle-struck city of Kherson, describing it as a deliberate “hunt” and “safari” targeting civilians.United Nations human rights monitors have raised concerns over the rising number of civilian casualties, which have reached their highest level since the war began in February 2022.
Article Summary: Russian airstrikes on the Ukrainian capital Kyiv killed 14 early on Wednesday morning. 27 others were injured as buildings and warehouses got damaged in a massive fire triggered by the strikes. The capital city of Ukraine experienced air raid alerts for over an hour and seven military sites were struck.

Article Title: 'Exploitation will never be tolerated': US sues Indian-origin landlord for 'sexually harassing' tenant
Article Text: An Indian-origin landlord in Pennsylvania, Venkatchalam Mani, is facing a federal lawsuit after the US Department of Justice accused him of sexually harassing a female tenant and retaliating against her when she rejected his alleged advances.The federal lawsuit filed on Wednesday in the US District Court for the Middle District of Pennsylvania, alleges that Venkatchalam Mani owner of a rental property in the State College borough, made repeated unwelcome sexual advances toward a female tenant, including unwanted sexual touching.According to the complaint, after the tenant rejected his advances, Mani allegedly ignored her repeated requests for maintenance, including repairing a broken furnace during the winter.The furnace later caught fire, forcing the woman and her family to leave the property."The landlord failed to fix a tenant's furnace despite freezing temperatures because the female tenant refused his sexual advances, forcing her family to move out with no other place to live," Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division said."This conduct is illegal. The Justice Department will uphold the rights of female tenants to housing without the threat of sexual harassment by a landlord," Dhillon added.The lawsuit seeks monetary compensation for the tenant and her children, along with a court order prohibiting Mani from engaging in similar discriminatory conduct in the future.US Attorney Brian D Miller for the Middle District of Pennsylvania said such behaviour would not be tolerated."Attempts to exploit tenants for sexual favours, sexual assault and retaliation by landlords will never be tolerated in the Middle District of Pennsylvania," Miller added.The case began after the tenant filed a complaint with the US Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), PTI reported. Following an investigation, HUD concluded that Mani had violated the Fair Housing Act and issued a charge of discrimination.After the tenant opted to have the matter heard in federal court, HUD referred the case to the Department of Justice, which subsequently filed the lawsuit.The Justice Department alleges that Mani's actions amounted to unlawful sexual harassment and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act and is seeking damages as well as an injunction to prevent future violations.
Article Summary: Venkatchalam Mani, an Indian-origin landlord in Pennsylvania, is facing a federal lawsuit after the US Department of Justice accused him of sexually harassing a female tenant. The federal lawsuit filed on Wednesday in the US District Court for the Middle District of Pennsylvania, alleges that Mani made repeated unwelcome sexual advances toward the woman.

Article Title: Trump says US has 'massive amounts' of munitions, warns action against 'leakers'
Article Text:
Trump dismisses munitions shortage claims, vows action against 'leakers'

US President Donald Trump on Thursday asserted that the United States has "massive amounts" of military munitions and said defence production is expanding rapidly, while warning that those responsible for leaking information about the country's weapons stockpiles would face legal action.In a post on Truth Social, Trump dismissed concerns over US munitions availability and said additional supplies were being manufactured and delivered as required."The US has massive amounts of “munitions,” especially of certain types. Additionally, large amounts are being manufactured and shipped to the US as needed. Defense companies are building the largest number of plants and factories in our country’s history. The “leakers” of these treasonous statements are being hunted down. Long term jail sentences will be sought!" Trump wrote.The remarks come amid reports questioning the state of US missile and ammunition stockpiles following months of military operations, including the conflict with Iran. Trump has repeatedly defended the country's military readiness and has sought to reassure allies about the US defence industrial base.His latest statement also signals a crackdown on officials accused of leaking sensitive information related to US military capabilities, with the president describing the alleged disclosures as "treasonous" and warning that authorities were pursuing those responsible.
Article Summary: Trump dismisses munitions shortage claims, vows action against 'leakers' US President Donald Trump on Thursday asserted that the United States has "massive amounts" of military munitions. Trump said defence production is expanding rapidly, while warning that those responsible for leaking information about the country's weapons stockpiles would face legal action.

Article Title: Trump turns toddler’s stage dash into Biden joke at Las Vegas event
Article Text:
Donald Trump at the Red Rock Casino Resort and Spa in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo: AP)

Trump invited Sandra and Brad, a Las Vegas couple, and their two young children on stage at the Red Rock Casino Resort and Spa while promoting his administration’s Trump Accounts and “no tax on tips” initiatives. The parents thanked him for the tax policy and the accounts for their children. Trump said Sandra worked as a waitress at a Las Vegas casino, while Brad served as an officer with the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department. He said the couple had benefited from his administration’s tax policies and were investing in Trump Accounts for both children. “It’s a beautiful family,” Trump said as they joined him on stage.Fox News reported that the toddler appeared ready to make a break for it as Sandra began addressing the crowd. Trump quickly reached out to prevent the child from leaving the stage. “I don't want him to be Biden and fall off the stage!” Trump said, drawing laughter from the audience.The family had another exchange with Trump later in the event. Sandra told him, “He did want to say a little something to you, Mr. President,” to which Trump replied, “Yes, thank you, thank you very much.” The toddler then babbled briefly before his mother softly prompted him, “Thank you for my Trump Account.”“Thank you for my Trump Account,” the boy repeated into the microphone, prompting an uproar of applause from the crowd. “Good job!” Trump said with a smile as he clapped for the toddler and the audience continued cheering. Trump is a father of five and has 11 grandchildren.
Article Summary: Trump invited Sandra and Brad, a Las Vegas couple, and their two young children on stage at the Red Rock Casino Resort and Spa. He said the couple had benefited from his administration’s tax policies and were investing in Trump Accounts for both children. Trump is a father of five and has 11 grandchildren.

Article Title: Did Trump and Hegseth clash over shrinking US missile stockpiles? White House responds
Article Text:
Camp David clash: Trump demanded answers from Hegseth over missile shortages - Report

US President Donald Trump confronted US defence secretary Pete Hegseth during a meeting at Camp David over severe shortages of key military munitions that have constrained Washington's options in the ongoing conflict with Iran, according to a report by The Washington Post. The report said Trump questioned why he had not been fully informed about depleted missile stockpiles, with the exchange highlighting growing tensions between the president and his defence chief.Citing two people familiar with the matter, the newspaper reported that Trump challenged Hegseth during a Cabinet meeting on Friday, saying he believed the munitions problem "had been fixed." The shortages, particularly of long-range precision-guided missiles and air defence interceptors, have become a key factor behind Trump's decision to hold back additional large-scale military strikes against Iran, according to one of the sources.The reported confrontation came days after Trump said he had ordered and later called off "the biggest attack since World War II" while citing fresh negotiations over the Strait of Hormuz.The report said the US military has rapidly depleted critical missile inventories during more than five months of fighting with Iran. In the first month of the conflict alone, US forces reportedly fired more than 850 Tomahawk cruise missiles, over 1,000 Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors, and more than 1,300 Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMS).One source told the newspaper the ATACMS stockpile has been exhausted to the point that "there's basically none left. "Meanwhile, white house spokesperson Karoline Leavitt in a post on X denied any such claims and said, "I was at Camp David with President Trump and Secretary Hegseth. This literally never happened, and we told the Washington Post that repeatedly. This B.S. story was shopped to many outlets by someone clearly out to disparage the Secretary, for whatever reason. Unfortunately for them, the President loves the Secretary and thinks he’s doing a tremendous job. "The shortages have also affected US support for Ukraine, which is facing dwindling air defence supplies as Western inventories shrink. According to the report, the scarcity of interceptor missiles has forced the Pentagon to change how it assesses whether incoming threats should be intercepted, depending on their trajectory and potential impact.The Washington Post reported that Hegseth defended himself during the Camp David meeting and blamed Deputy Defence Secretary Stephen Feinberg for failing to ensure Trump was fully briefed on the extent of the shortages.The White House and Pentagon strongly denied the report."This is 100% fake news. Literally never happened. And President Trump has the utmost confidence in Secretary Hegseth," White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt said.Pentagon chief spokesman Sean Parnell also rejected the claims."Secretary Hegseth did not mislead anyone about our munitions posture, and he did not blame Deputy Secretary Feinberg. These claims about depleted stockpiles, internal disagreements, the Secretary’s position on Iran … are equally fictional," Parnell said.The report said the Camp David exchange reflected Trump's growing frustration with Hegseth, who had been among the strongest advocates for military action against Iran and reportedly argued that the campaign would be swift and relatively straightforward.The administration is now seeking additional funding to replenish US military inventories. Hegseth, Feinberg and Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine have asked Congress for an additional $67 billion to cover the costs of the Iran conflict and rebuild depleted stockpiles. Hegseth previously described the funding request as an "urgent, necessary" requirement, although Senate Republicans have yet to agree on a strategy to advance the package.According to the report, the Pentagon's proposed $1.5 trillion defence budget for the next fiscal year includes tens of billions of dollars for missile production. However, the spending plan has stalled in Congress amid opposition from Democrats, delaying efforts to replenish critical weapons inventories.The report noted that rebuilding the arsenal will take years despite new production agreements announced by the Pentagon. Patriot interceptors and other advanced munitions require lengthy manufacturing timelines, with defence experts warning that production cannot accelerate without congressional appropriations and signed contracts."aren’t going to start bending metal until you have a contract and congressional appropriations," Brad Bowman, senior director at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told The Washington Post."We’re often talking years between spending what we need to spend, getting the contracts signed, and delivery," he added. "You don’t just flip the switch and suddenly the munition appears in the hands of the warfighter."
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump confronted US defence secretary Pete Hegseth during a meeting at Camp David, according to a report. Trump questioned why he had not been fully informed about depleted missile stockpiles, the report said. The White House and Pentagon strongly denied the report."This is 100% fake news. Literally never happened," a White House spokesperson said.

Article Title: $150 million contract for migrant children's lawyers goes to Trump-linked firm
Article Text:
Trump’s $150M legal contract for migrant children sparks concerns (Photo: White House Gallery)

What is known about Burke Law Group?

What legal protections apply to migrant children?

Why did lawyers’ emails and court appearances cause confusion?

A Houston law firm with ties to the Trump administration and little experience in immigration law has been awarded a $150 million contract to represent migrant children travelling alone to the US.The contract was awarded to the small Houston-based Burke Law Group as the Trump administration intensifies its mass deportation campaign across the country. It comes after the administration allowed a key contract with a nationwide network of legal groups assisting immigrant children to expire last week without a replacement. Providers have increasingly warned that children may not receive experienced legal assistance as the administration steps up efforts to remove people from the country.The Associated Press reported that Michael Lukens, who heads the Amica Center, described the decision to award the sole-source contract to the Texas firm as “upsetting and shocking”. “It really does forebode a situation where children are going to get no meaningful due process, no meaningful day in court. We cannot have a random law firm entrusted to take care of children,” Lukens said.The contract announced on Tuesday covers only children currently held in government-run shelters, according to the legal aid groups.The government would need to issue another contract to cover services for migrant children living outside the shelter system. Lukens said about 1,800 children were currently living in shelters, while roughly 22,000 were living outside them with sponsors such as family members.The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) oversees the government agency responsible for caring for unaccompanied migrant children. The department did not respond to requests for comment. The Trump administration announced late on Tuesday that it was hiring Burke Law Group to provide legal services to unaccompanied children.The contract will run for one year and starts on August 15. Only two of the 25 lawyers listed on the firm’s website on Wednesday morning claimed relevant experience in immigration law in their biographies. Many of the other lawyers at the firm are corporate lawyers with ties to conservative causes and President Donald Trump.Marcella Burke, the firm’s founder, served as a lawyer in the Environmental Protection Agency and the Department of the Interior during Trump’s first administration. The firm’s roster also includes Justin Shubow, the leading supporter of Trump’s efforts to require federal buildings to follow classical and traditional architectural styles. Shubow is also a former Trump appointee to the US Commission of Fine Arts.Prominent conservative legal scholar Ilya Shapiro is listed by the firm as a “senior counsel”. Burke Law Group and its founder did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment. The contract notice describes the arrangement as a “single source cooperative agreement”.The designation means the administration selected the firm without a competitive bidding process. The notice did not provide a justification for bypassing standard bidding rules. No competitive process for selecting the firm was described in the notice.Migrant children travelling without an accompanying adult are considered particularly vulnerable because of their age and are usually placed in US government care. Several legal protections apply to them after they enter the country. These include the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008, which requires the government to facilitate legal representation for children placed in deportation proceedings.Until recently, that representation was provided by a network of nearly 100 legal aid organizations across the country. The providers conducted know-your-rights training for children in shelters and represented them directly in court proceedings. Last Friday marked the final day of that contract.Until late Tuesday, it remained unclear whether a replacement contract would be awarded and, if so, which organization would carry out the work. The legal aid providers have also said they have struggled to obtain payment for work completed since last November. They said the administration has requested detailed information about their clients that they are ethically unable to provide.Legal advocates have reported other developments that have caused concern. Since April, courts have begun calling dozens of cases at once in proceedings described as “rocket dockets”. Immigrant children have also had their hearings moved forward and been given less time to prepare.Other recent developments have raised questions about the administration’s intentions regarding the children’s legal representation and caused confusion. The Associated Press obtained emails sent late on Tuesday by the Office of Refugee Resettlement, the federal agency responsible for overseeing unaccompanied migrant children. The messages were sent to lawyers representing migrant children in federal custody.The emails asked the lawyers for their clients’ personal identification numbers. They also asked them to respond within four hours and confirm that they would appear to represent their clients at upcoming hearings. It was not immediately clear why the administration was making such requests of the children’s lawyers.Separately, attorneys in courtrooms across the country said their hearings were interrupted by lawyers claiming the Trump administration had asked them to take over the children’s cases without giving prior notice. One such incident occurred during a Chicago hearing on Wednesday morning for unaccompanied immigrant children in detention. A lawyer who did not represent any of the children suddenly appeared through a video stream in an exchange witnessed by an Associated Press reporter.The lawyer said she was with the US Committee for Refugees and Immigrants, a legal aid organization. She said the Office of Refugee Resettlement had contacted the organization to “appear on behalf” of children without legal representation because of a “gap in legal services”. She also said the federal government had provided the organization with the children’s private information, including their names and identification numbers.The judge said all the children already had lawyers and refused to allow anyone else to watch through the video stream. The outside lawyer then disconnected from the hearing. Laura Smith, an attorney representing some of the children, expressed confusion about the lawyer’s presence, saying: “It sounds like this is a person who has my client’s information.”The US Committee for Refugees and Immigrants referred questions from the Associated Press to HHS’s Office of Refugee Resettlement. Alexa Sendukas, managing attorney at the Galveston Houston Immigrant Representation Project, said one of her organization’s lawyers witnessed similar confusion in a Houston courtroom on Wednesday morning. She said the organization had also heard about comparable situations in other courtrooms across the country.
Article Summary: The contract was awarded to the small Houston-based Burke Law Group. It comes after the administration allowed a key contract with a nationwide network of legal groups assisting immigrant children to expire last week. Providers have increasingly warned that children may not receive experienced legal assistance as the administration steps up efforts to remove people from the country.

Article Title: Why was a plane allowed to take off as Trump's helicopter approached
Article Text:
The incident took place on Tuesday as Marine One carried Trump from the White House to Andrews Air Force Base for the first leg of his West Coast trip

What happened over Reagan National Airport

Why is the incident drawing scrutiny

The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is investigating why a commercial aircraft was cleared for take-off from Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport while US President Donald Trump's helicopter, Marine One, was approaching the airport, despite safety procedures introduced after last year's deadly midair collision.The incident took place on Tuesday as Marine One carried Trump from the White House to Andrews Air Force Base for the first leg of his West Coast trip. Although officials said the aircraft were never on a collision course and the president was never in danger, the event has raised fresh questions about whether the stricter safety measures introduced after January 2025's fatal crash are being properly followed.Both the FAA and the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) are gathering information about the incident. While the FAA has launched a preliminary investigation, the NTSB said it was still assessing the circumstances before deciding whether to open a separate probe.According to the FAA, the commercial jet took off as Marine One was approaching Reagan National Airport. The plane climbed above the presidential helicopter, meaning the two aircraft were moving apart rather than towards one another.Even so, the FAA said there was a "momentary loss of separation" between the aircraft.Air traffic controllers remained in contact with both the airline crew and the Marine One pilots throughout the incident.The agency has not explained why the commercial flight was authorised to depart while Marine One was inbound. The Wall Street Journal first reported the incident.The White House sought to reassure the public, saying Trump was never at risk. "Marine One flights are piloted by some of the best aviators in the world, and at no point was the President in harm's way," White House spokesperson Kush Desai said.The US Marine Corps also rejected suggestions of a near miss. Spokesperson Capt. Jacob Sugg said there were no "close calls" and that controllers neither delayed nor altered the helicopter's flight path, instead providing appropriate traffic information throughout the journey.The investigation comes just months after a catastrophic collision on 29 January 2025, when a passenger airliner and a US Army Black Hawk helicopter crashed near Reagan National Airport, killing all 67 people aboard the two aircraft.Following that disaster, the FAA introduced stricter operating procedures for the airport's notoriously congested airspace. The rules require all take-offs and landings to be suspended whenever helicopters travel along conflicting routes near the airport. Controllers are also required to use radar rather than visual separation, while military aircraft must continuously broadcast their locations.The latest incident has prompted renewed criticism from families of those killed in last year's crash, who questioned whether enough has been been done to improve safety around Reagan National. The group has continued to urge Congress to adopt aviation safety reforms recommended by the NTSB.
Article Summary: The incident took place on Tuesday as Marine One carried Trump from the White House to Andrews Air Force Base for the first leg of his West Coast trip. Officials said the aircraft were never on a collision course and the president was never in danger. The incident has raised fresh questions about whether the stricter safety measures introduced after January 2025's fatal crash are being properly followed.

Article Title: Jill Biden says Joe Biden 'will forever live with cancer,' reveals he was waking up seven times a night before prostate cancer diagnosis
Article Text:
Jill Biden says Joe Biden 'will forever live with cancer,' reveals he was waking up seven times a night before prostate cancer diagnosis

Diagnosis came after leaving the White House

Jill says she never suspected prostate cancer

Kelly Ripa pushes back against 'cover-up' claims

Former US First Lady Jill Biden has shared new details about former President Joe Biden 's health, revealing that he was waking up "seven times a night" before he was diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer.Speaking on SiriusXM's Let's Talk Off Camera with Kelly Ripa on Wednesday, Jill Biden said she had repeatedly raised concerns with White House physicians about her husband's frequent nighttime trips but believed the issue had already been addressed."I thought it was addressed," she said, recalling how she had informed doctors about Joe Biden's condition while they were still in the White House.However, after leaving the White House in January 2025, the problem persisted."But when it continued when we got out of the White House, I said, 'Joe, we've got to go up to Jeff in Philly — something's wrong,'" Jill said during the interview.Joe Biden, 83, was diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer in May 2025. The disease had already spread to his bones by the time it was detected.Jill said the former president will have to live with the illness permanently."He will forever live with cancer," she said, adding that his treatment now involves regular monitoring every three months, along with medication."We have to be mindful of it every three months, testing and medicines. And anybody who's gone through this cancer journey... it's constant. It's daily. And I think it's challenging," she said.Jill also reflected on her family's previous experience with cancer, mentioning the loss of Beau Biden, Joe Biden's eldest son, who died from glioblastoma in 2015.Despite sensing that something was wrong, Jill admitted she never imagined prostate cancer would be the diagnosis."I never, oh my God, I never thought it would be prostate cancer," she said.Earlier, in a May 2025 interview with CBS Sunday Morning, Jill had described the diagnosis as "shocking," saying she was surprised that the condition had not been detected despite the extensive medical care available to the president while he was in office.According to Joe Biden's physician, routine PSA blood screening for prostate cancer is generally not recommended for men over 70 under the American Urological Association's guidelines, as the disease is often slow-growing.Podcast host Kelly Ripa also addressed speculation suggesting the Biden family had concealed the diagnosis, saying such assumptions ignore how difficult bone cancer can be to detect early.Ripa shared that her own father discovered cancer only after a car accident led doctors to investigate persistent back pain."So when people were like, 'There's no way you can't know,' oh, yes, there is," Ripa said.In addition to his prostate cancer treatment, a spokesperson confirmed in September 2025 that Joe Biden also underwent Mohs surgery, a procedure commonly used to treat skin cancer.Jill concluded the interview on a hopeful note, saying that although the cancer cannot be eliminated, her husband is "doing okay."
Article Summary: Former US First Lady Jill Biden spoke on SiriusXM's Let's Talk Off Camera with Kelly Ripa on Wednesday. She said she had repeatedly raised concerns with White House physicians about her husband's frequent nighttime trips. Joe Biden, 83, was diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer in May 2025.

Article Title: Utah nurse thought woman was drowning until he saw the blood and realized it was a fatal shark attack; did everything he could to save her
Article Text:
Utah nurse thought woman was drowning until he saw the blood and realized it was a fatal shark attack; did everything he could to save her

'I thought someone was drowning'

A routine snorkeling trip turns tragic

'I saw the blood and immediately knew'

Tried to save her until the very end
