Husband pays emotional tribute

'She wasn't alone in the end'

A registered nurse from Utah has shared the harrowing details of trying to save a woman who was fatally attacked by a shark while snorkeling in the Caribbean, revealing that he initially believed she was drowning before discovering the true horror unfolding in the water.Chris Carroll, 56, was relaxing with his wife on the balcony of their hotel in St. Croix after a day of scuba diving when he heard frantic screams coming from the beach below.Carroll, who is also a former lifeguard and director of surgical services at Holy Cross Hospital – Mountain Point in Lehi, Utah, said he heard people shouting, "Where are the lifeguards?""It was just a typical rural Caribbean beach," Carroll told People. "There are no lifeguards."Believing someone was drowning, Carroll immediately sprinted toward the water. Unbeknownst to him, beachgoers were actually warning swimmers to get out of the sea after spotting a shark.At the same time, 56-year-old Arlene Lillis and her husband Richard were snorkeling off Dorsch Beach, one of their favourite vacation spots in St. Croix.According to Carroll, the couple's heads were underwater, preventing them from hearing the desperate warnings from people on the shore.While Richard continued swimming along the reef, Arlene stopped behind to take a closer look at something underwater. It was during those moments that she was attacked by a shark.Carroll estimated that Arlene was around 50 to 75 yards from shore when he spotted her slapping the surface of the water."I dove in and started swimming," he recalled."I asked, 'Are you OK?' and then I saw the blood and immediately had a shock of fear go through me, because I realized in that moment this isn't a drowning. This is a shark attack."Although he knew the predator could still be nearby, Carroll said leaving her behind never crossed his mind."I knew in my heart and soul that I couldn't leave her."He stayed beside Arlene, reassuring her that help was coming while other beachgoers assisted in bringing her back to shore.As emergency responders arrived, Carroll briefed them on the severity of Arlene's injuries and the urgent medical care she required to manage the massive blood loss.Despite their efforts, Arlene succumbed to her injuries. The Virgin Islands Police Department later confirmed her death.The tragedy deeply affected Carroll, who said he later learned that Richard was unaware of what had happened until he returned to the beach, where police informed him of his wife's death.Following the tragedy, Richard remembered Arlene as a loving wife, mother and grandmother."She was so beautiful inside and out! She will be missed every second of the day," he wrote in a heartfelt tribute.In a later social media post, he shared that the family had scattered her ashes in the ocean.The incident continued to haunt Carroll, who admitted he struggled with returning to the water even days later."Ultimately, I knew that if I don't get back in the water, I'm never going to get back in the water. So I chose to go," he said of attending a scheduled scuba diving class after the attack."But I'd be lying if I said I was warm and fuzzy the whole time. I was diving. I was looking over my shoulder a lot."A few days after the attack, Carroll received an unexpected phone call from Arlene's daughter.Instead of questioning his actions, she thanked him for staying with her mother during her final moments and apologised for the trauma he had endured while trying to save her."I'll never know Arlene, but the kind of people who loved her showed real character," Carroll said."She mentioned that her mom hated to be alone and that even though I couldn't save her, she wasn't alone in the end. There was somebody there holding onto her and comforting her."Carroll said those words helped ease the guilt and "what ifs" that had weighed heavily on him since the tragedy."I wish I could have done more, but that wasn't the case," he reflected. "I just want people to remember we're all connected. You probably won't ever be asked to swim out to someone attacked by a shark, but you can always reach out to people who are struggling."
Article Summary: Chris Carroll, 56, was relaxing with his wife on the balcony of their hotel in St. Croix when he heard frantic screams coming from the beach below. Arlene Lillis and her husband Richard were snorkeling off Dorsch Beach, one of their favourite vacation spots in the Caribbean. Unbeknownst to him, beachgoers were warning swimmers to get out of the sea after spotting a shark. Carroll estimated that Arlene was around 50 to 75 yards from shore when he spotted her slapping the surface.

Article Title: West American dams are on the verge of shutting down: Lack of maintenance is filling them with silt faster than ever, making the great structures obsolete
Article Text:
Shihmen Reservoir releasing sediment through the power plant discharge outlet. Image Credit: Peellden

How big is the scale of dam sedimentation in the American West

How sediment accumulation has been affecting the Lake Mead

Sediment-laden water from the Colorado River flowing into Lake Mead in March 2013. Image Credit: NASA

What are the environmental costs of trapping river sediment

What strategies exist for future sediment maintenance

Removal of the Marmot Dam, Sandy River, Oregon. Image Credit: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration(NOAA)

Climate change complicating the preservation of dams

The accumulation of sediment in reservoirs across the American West represents a significant challenge for water resource management. Since the early 20th century, thousands of dams have been constructed to provide essential services, including hydro-electric power, irrigation for agriculture, and reliable municipal water supplies. However, these structures naturally trap the silt, sand, and clay carried by rivers.As these materials settle, they gradually affect the water storage capacity that is important for the survival of communities in arid regions. A major portion of global reservoir capacity is being lost annually, creating a long-term threat to infrastructure. In the western United States, where aging dams and shifting climate patterns are common, the management of this crisis has become a priority for federal agencies.According to the document titled ‘ Sediment Bypassing – Preserving America’s Reservoirs ,’ the United States has built and currently relies upon over 92,000 dams and reservoirs. These structures are vital for everything from municipal use to flood risk reduction, but their ability to function is being disturbed by the very rivers they built on.In the report ‘ A Watershed Moment for Western U.S. Dams ,’ researchers Amy E. East and Gordon E. Grant points out that since 1990, the amount of water storage capacity lost to sedimentation has outpaced the gains made by building new dams.When accounting for a growing population, water storage available per person in the United States has dropped by 35% since 1970. This suggests that the infrastructure growth of the last century is reaching a point where maintenance is more critical than new construction. As noted in the book chapter ‘ Dams, Rivers, and the Environment ,’ millions of dams have fragmented the Earth’s landscapes globally, and many are now permanent components of the environment that must be managed sustainably to prevent complete failure.The ‘ 2001 Lake Mead Sedimentation Survey ’ produced by the US Bureau of Reclamation reveals that since the Hoover dam was completed in 1935, the reservoir has seen 2.4 million acre-feet of sediment deposition. To understand easily, an acre-foot is roughly the amount of water needed to cover a football pitch to a depth of one foot. Interestingly, the 2001 survey actually measured an increase in the reservoir's capacity since the previous check in 1963.This phenomenon was not due to the removal of silt, but because of the closure of Glen Canyon Dam further upstream. As explained in the Bureau of Reclamation’s technical appendix ‘ TA 5. Geomorphology and Sediment ,’ the closure of Glen Canyon Dam in 1963 cut off approximately 95% of the historical sediment supply that used to flow into Lake Mead. The sediment already present in Lake Mead had nearly four decades to settle into a smaller volume, while very little new material arrived to take its place.By trapping silt and sand, dams are cutting off downstream supply of sediments required for healthy ecosystems. ‘A Watershed Moment for Western U.S. Dams’ report notes that the lack of sand floods in the Grand Canyon has led to the erosion of sandbars and the exposure of irreplaceable archaeological sites that were once protected by wind-blown sand.Furthermore, the technical appendix highlights that because the Colorado River now transports sand downstream faster than tributaries can resupply it, there has been erosion of channel and sandbar deposits since 1963. This ‘sediment starvation’ simplifies the river’s shape and limits the formation of habitats necessary for native fish and wildlife. The trapping of sediments results in the lowering of river beds and the loss of wetlands, which are essential for flood-resistance and supporting biodiversity.One strategy is ‘water injection dredging’ which is a cost-effective and environmentally sound technique. This method involves injecting large volumes of water into the sediment layer at low pressure to liquefy it, allowing the resulting mixture to flow along the bottom and remain within the natural river system instead of filling up a disposal site.Additionally, as structures become obsolete or unsafe due to excessive silt, dam removal is becoming a more frequent strategy. ‘A Watershed Moment for Western U.S. Dams’ report points to the historic removal project on the Klamath River as a sign of a changing paradigm in water management. For the remaining dams, strategies such as ‘sediment sluicing’(opening gates during flood events to let muddy water pass through) are being used in places like Asia and Europe to extend the life of these reservoirs.As detailed in ‘A Watershed Moment for Western U.S. Dams’ increasing temperatures are leading to more frequent and intense wildfires. When a landscape is scorched by fire, the soil loses its grip and subsequent rains then wash massive amounts of debris and sediment into downstream reservoirs.In California alone, post-fire erosion has increased significantly, with over half of that sediment ending up in reservoirs. This creates a difficult cycle where reservoirs are filling fast, just when they are needed the most to manage the water supplies caused by a warming world.
Article Summary: Since the early 20th century, thousands of dams have been constructed to provide essential services, including hydro-electric power, irrigation for agriculture, and reliable municipal water supplies. These structures naturally trap the silt, sand, and clay carried by rivers. As these materials settle, they affect the water storage capacity that is important for the survival of communities in arid regions.

Article Title: In 2023, America’s first live yellow-legged hornet, a bee-killing predator, was found in Georgia; by 2026, officials had trapped 866 and destroyed 44 nests
Article Text:
Georgia officials trap 866 invasive yellow-legged hornets, eradicate 44 nests this year

Early spring emergence and growing nest threat

State agriculture chief calls for public help

Birds provide only limited natural control

State agriculture teams in Georgia have trapped at least 866 invasive yellow-legged hornets and destroyed 44 active nests so far this year, according to official data released by the Georgia Department of Agriculture.The figures, listed on the state's public yellow-legged hornet eradication dashboard, show the latest progress in an intensive control campaign that began after the first live specimen of the bee-killing insect was confirmed in Georgia in 2023.The invasive pest, which is native to Southeast Asia, poses a major threat to natural pollinators, farm crops, and food production across the southern United States.State officials said the hornets have been confirmed in five Georgia counties this year: Bryan, Bulloch, Chatham, Effingham, and Liberty.The scale of the eradication effort remains significant. Data published by the Georgia Department of Agriculture shows officials dealt with a total of 95,530 yellow-legged hornets across the state during 2025 alone.The yellow-legged hornet, scientifically known as Vespa velutina, grows to about two centimetres in length. It has a dark, slim body, yellow-tipped legs, and a clear yellow band on its fourth abdominal segment.Although it is often compared with the larger northern giant hornet, the yellow-legged hornet creates a different ecological risk because of the way it hunts and how quickly it reproduces.The species comes out of winter hibernation in early spring, when fertilized queens build small primary nests. If these early nests are not destroyed, the queens continue producing worker hornets through the summer. This allows colonies to grow rapidly into much larger secondary nests by late summer and autumn.Recent inspections by the Georgia Department of Agriculture's Plant Protection Division found an increase in "hawking" behaviour near domestic beehives.Hawking happens when adult hornets hover outside honeybee hives and attack worker bees as they return carrying nectar and pollen. Transport experts and entomologists say this behaviour shows that hornet colonies have entered the important secondary nesting stage.The loss of honeybees threatens commercial fruit, nut, and vegetable crops that depend on insect pollination, increasing concerns among farmers across the region. Sightings of the yellow-legged hornet have also been reported in neighbouring states, including South Carolina and Alabama.As secondary nests continue appearing high in trees, state officials are asking residents and landowners to help by reporting suspected hornet activity.In a public statement, Georgia Department of Agriculture Commissioner Tyler J. Harper stressed that community support is essential to stop the pest from becoming permanently established."Georgia has made significant progress in tracking and eliminating the Yellow-legged Hornet, but our success depends on continued public support," said Georgia Department of Agriculture Commissioner Tyler J. Harper. "The sooner a nest is identified and reported, the sooner our team can respond. We are asking every Georgian to remain vigilant and help us keep this invasive species from gaining a foothold in our state. "State guidance advises people to look for large, round or oval paper-like nests made from layers of grey or brown pulp. These secondary nests are usually found high in tree branches or under the eaves of buildings and often remain visible through late summer and winter.Officials also ask residents who see hornets hovering near beehives, especially before noon or after 5 p.m., to record the location and report it immediately.The department strongly advises people not to remove or destroy hornet nests themselves. If a nest is not completely destroyed, the queen may escape and start a new colony elsewhere. Instead, suspected sightings should be reported to the Plant Protection Division or a licensed pest control professional so the entire colony, including the queen, can be safely eliminated.As wildlife experts look at long-term control options, questions have been raised about whether native birds can help reduce yellow-legged hornet numbers.In an analysis published by ornithology magazine Birds & Blooms, naturalists Kenn and Kimberly Kaufman discussed whether native birds prey on paper-nest wasps and hornets.They explained that birds rarely hunt active adult wasps or hornets during summer because of the danger of being stung. However, some bird species feed on nests after cold weather arrives."Bald-faced hornets build nests of gray paperlike material, made from chewed-up bits of wood. They use them for only one season. As cold weather approaches, the queen hornet leaves to spend the winter in hibernation elsewhere. The other adult hornets, as well as the last larvae and pupae, remain in the nest. There, they grow sluggish and eventually freeze to death. Once they're immobilized, various birds may rip open the nest to eat the hornets inside. This has been documented for blue jays, woodpeckers and others," Kenn and Kimberly Kaufman wrote in Birds & Blooms.The naturalists added that intelligent birds such as blue jays have also been seen knocking adult stinging insects to the ground before eating them and tearing open smaller paper nests to feed on the protein-rich larvae.However, state entomologists say this seasonal bird activity is not enough to stop the spread of invasive yellow-legged hornets during their active summer breeding season. Careful monitoring, public reporting, and targeted nest removal remain the main methods for eliminating the species from Georgia.
Article Summary: The invasive pest poses a major threat to natural pollinators, farm crops, and food production across the southern United States. Sightings of the yellow- legged hornet have also been reported in neighbouring states, including South Carolina and Alabama. The species comes out of winter hibernation in early spring, when fertilized queens build small primary nests.

Article Title: Commercial plane takes off as Trump’s helicopter nears airport; FAA investigates
Article Text:
Marine One, with President Donald Trump onboard near Trump National Golf Club Los Angeles

The Federal Aviation Administration is investigating a possible safety violation after a commercial plane took off from Reagan National Airport while President Donald Trump ’s helicopter, Marine One, was approaching the airport on Tuesday.The incident happened as Marine One was flying from the White House to Andrews Air Force Base, carrying Trump for the first leg of a West Coast trip. The commercial aircraft took off at around the same time and climbed above the approaching helicopter.The FAA said the two aircraft were not on a collision course but acknowledged a “momentary loss of separation”. “The air traffic controller was in contact with both the commercial pilot and Marine One pilot during the loss of separation,” the agency said, as quoted by Reuters.The incident is significant because the FAA had introduced stricter procedures at Reagan National Airport after a midair collision on January 29, 2025, killed 67 people. Under the rules, all takeoffs and landings at the airport are supposed to be halted whenever a helicopter passes nearby.The FAA has not said why the commercial aircraft was cleared to take off while Marine One was approaching. It is investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident.The White House said Trump was not in danger. “Marine One flights are piloted by some of the best aviators in the world, and at no point was the President in harm’s way,” White House spokesman Kush Desai said.The Marine Corps also rejected suggestions that the helicopter came close to the plane. “There were no ‘close calls’ with the routine Marine One movement,” Marine Corps spokesman Capt. Jacob Sugg said.Sugg said Washington National Tower did not delay or ask the helicopter crew to hold and instead “approved the requested route and provided timely and appropriate traffic information.”The Wall Street Journal first reported the incident.The airspace around the White House and Reagan National Airport is heavily congested, with military and commercial aircraft operating in close proximity. Following last year’s crash, the FAA moved to prevent helicopters and airplanes from sharing the same airspace around Reagan. The rules also prohibit controllers from relying on visual separation and require military aircraft to broadcast their locations.Families of victims of last year’s crash questioned whether enough has been done to improve safety in the crowded airspace. They have urged Congress to pass aviation safety reforms recommended by the National Transportation Safety Board.The NTSB said it was still gathering information about Tuesday’s incident and had not yet decided whether to open its own investigation.
Article Summary: A commercial plane took off from Reagan National Airport while President Donald Trump ’s helicopter, Marine One, was approaching the airport on Tuesday. The FAA said the two aircraft were not on a collision course but acknowledged a “momentary loss of separation’

Article Title: Indian-American Congressman Shri Thanedar loses Democratic primary in Michigan
Article Text:
File photo: Indian-American Congressman Shri Thanedar

Progressive wing scores another victory

Thanedar faced multiple challenges during campaign

Indian-American representation in House may decline

Indian-American Congressman Shri Thanedar lost the Democratic primary in Michigan's 13th Congressional District on Tuesday, with state Representative Donavan McKinney defeating the two-term lawmaker in a closely fought contest backed by the Democratic Party's progressive wing.McKinney secured 51.9 per cent of the vote against Thanedar's 48.1 per cent, winning by a margin of 3.79 percentage points.The news agency Associated Press called the race at 9:55 am EDT.McKinney will now become the Democratic nominee for the November House of Representatives election from the heavily Democratic district, where he is considered the favourite to win.McKinney, a 34-year-old state legislator, was backed by several prominent progressive leaders and organisations, including Senator Bernie Sanders, Representative Rashida Tlaib, Justice Democrats and Leaders We Deserve.According to NBC News, the victory marks another success for the Democratic Party's progressive faction, which has been mounting primary challenges against establishment-backed incumbents.McKinney campaigned on a progressive platform that included "Medicare for All", increased investments in clean energy and housing, and tighter restrictions on US military aid to Israel.Both candidates supported several progressive policies, including universal healthcare and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).However, McKinney sharply criticised Israel's military campaign in Gaza, describing it as a "genocide", while Thanedar consistently voted in favour of military aid to Israel.Thanedar acknowledged the broader political trend after the result."The socialist movement that has defeated many sitting members in New York and elsewhere has come to Michigan, and we came out short," he told The New York Times, while pledging to support McKinney in the general election.Thanedar initially identified as a progressive but later distanced himself from the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) in 2023.During the campaign, he also faced criticism from fellow Democrats after introducing articles of impeachment against President Donald Trump without backing from the party leadership.Thanedar's campaign came under scrutiny over financial decisions, including reported losses of more than $2 million linked to cryptocurrency investments and the use of taxpayer-funded television advertisements that resembled campaign ads.Despite those controversies, Thanedar received endorsements from House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries and other senior House Democrats.Thanedar's defeat is likely to reduce Indian-American representation in the US House of Representatives from six to four, assuming Representatives Ro Khanna, Ami Bera, Pramila Jayapal and Suhas Subramanyam retain their seats in November.Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi will not return to the House after unsuccessfully contesting the Senate Democratic primary earlier this year.Meanwhile, Indian-American candidate Amish Shah is the Democratic nominee from Arizona's First Congressional District for the November election, while Pia Dandiya remains in the race for the Democratic primary in Florida.Thanedar, who immigrated to the United States from India in 1979 to pursue a PhD in chemistry, reflected on his political journey after the defeat."This country has given me so much, including an ability to represent 750,000 people in the United States Congress. That has been the honour of my life," he told The New York Times.Asked about his future plans, Thanedar said he intended to remain active in public life."I did not have a plan B... I will continue to stay involved and continue to help serve the people of my district," he said.
Article Summary: Indian-American Congressman Shri Thanedar lost the Democratic primary in Michigan's 13th Congressional District on Tuesday. State Representative Donavan McKinney defeated the two-term lawmaker in a closely fought contest backed by the Democratic Party's progressive wing. McKinney will now become the Democratic nominee for the November House of Representatives election from the heavily Democratic district.

Article Title: America edges towards first Muslim Senator as Michigan backs progressive rebel
Article Text:
Abdul El-Sayed will face Republican Mike Rogers in November

TOI correspondent from Washington:

The United States is edging towards its first ever Muslim Senator after Abdul El-Sayed, an Egyptian-American physician, Rhodes scholar, podcaster and progressive insurgent, defeated the Democratic establishment backed four-term Representative Haley Stevens in one of the most closely watched and bitterly fought primaries of the 2026 election cycle. If he goes on to defeat Republican Mike Rogers in November, El-Sayed will break one of the last symbolic barriers in American politics, which has not seen a Muslim elected to the Senate in the 250 years after the republic's founding.El-Sayed victory, coming amid a MAGA-infused America, is about much more than Michigan; it is another unmistakable sign that even the Democratic Party's restless grassroots increasingly resembles an unruly family reunion where the children have wrestled the remote control away from the parents. While the old guard still command the cheque books, newcomers are increasingly winning the applause and the votes, and so it was on Tuesday night when persistence of the son of Egyptian immigrants' trumped patronage of the establishment.El-Sayed, who was born near Detroit, accumulated degrees from the University of Michigan, Columbia and Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar before leading Detroit's health department. He first burst onto the national political scene in 2018 during an unsuccessful gubernatorial bid, but instead of disappearing into consulting or cable television, he plodded through retail politics, patiently building a progressive political network across Michigan.His party rival Stevens enjoyed endorsements from Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Governor Gretchen Whitmer, outgoing Senator Gary Peters and much of the Democratic establishment. Outside groups, including pro-Israel outfits, poured tens of millions of dollars into supporting her campaign. Outspent, El-Sayed countered with volunteers, small donors, Bernie Sanders, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Elizabeth Warren, and an argument that corporate money has corrupted America.The ideological fault lines running through today's Democratic Party were visible in almost every issue that defined the campaign. El-Sayed advocated Medicare for All, higher taxes on the wealthy, removing corporate money from politics and ending U.S. military aid to Israel, describing the Gaza war as genocide. Stevens offered a more centrist, pragmatic message built around manufacturing, electability and traditional Democratic coalition-building. The contest became a proxy war over Israel, campaign finance, and the party's future identity.Progressive victories over establishment Democrats have become increasingly common in safely Democratic urban districts from Berkeley to Brooklyn. But winning a statewide Senate primary in one of America's premier battleground states like Michigan is a different deal altogether. It suggests that progressive economics, anti-establishment populism and skepticism toward corporate influence are finding traction beyond the party's coastal strongholds. Michigan is perhaps the clearest indication yet that progressive candidates can no longer be dismissed as niche activists appealing only to deep-blue enclaves.The broader historical rhythm is also hard to ignore. Barack Obama's election in 2008 symbolized a generational and demographic transformation that convinced many Americans the country had entered a new political era. But it also intensified partisan polarization and ultimately contributed to Trump's populist victory in 2016. American politics has spent much of the last decade oscillating between those competing visions. It now appears the pendulum may be swinging back again.El-Sayed's nomination reflects not only America's growing diversity but also the frustration of younger Democrats with incrementalism, inequality and institutions they increasingly regard as captured by wealthy interests. The Establishment argues such candidates risk alienating swing voters; rebels counter that cautious centrism has produced too many narrow defeats and too little inspiration. Whether Michigan becomes proof of progressive electability or merely another fascinating primary upset will be decided in November, when El-Sayed faces Trump-backed Republican Mike Rogers in a race likely to determine control of the Senate.For now, though, one conclusion is unavoidable: The Democratic bosses may still own the party's furniture, but insurgents have begun rearranging the house. And judging by Michigan, they're no longer asking permission before moving the sofa.
Article Summary: Abdul El-Sayed, an Egyptian-American physician, Rhodes scholar, podcaster and progressive insurgent, defeated the Democratic establishment backed four-term Representative Haley Stevens. If he goes on to defeat Republican Mike Rogers in November, he will break one of the last symbolic barriers in American politics, which has not seen a Muslim elected to the Senate in 250 years.

Article Title: Imran Khan's three years in jail spark protests across Pakistan; over 100 held
Article Text:
More than 100 supporters of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan have been arrested as rallies were held across Pakistan on Wednesday to mark the completion of three years of his imprisonment.

Peshawar rally sets September 27 deadline

Family, PTI leaders raise detention concerns

Over 100 supporters of jailed former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan were arrested on Wednesday as Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) supporters held rallies nationwide to mark three years of his imprisonment. The demonstrations, which called for Khan’s release, saw police fire tear gas at protesters in Rawalpindi amid clashes and heightened security.The main rally was held in Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where PTI is in power. The party demanded Khan’s release and restoration of his rights. Thousands of supporters gathered amid heavy security, according to Al Jazeera.In Punjab, Police baton-charged protesters and arresting scores of PTI workers in Lahore, Mianwali and Rawalpindi. In Lahore's Mall Road, police dispersed demonstrators demanding Khan's release and detained several protesters.Video footage circulated on social media showed rapid response force (RRF) using force against demonstrators. Some journalists covering the rally were also allegedly thrashed by police, prompting protests from media bodies.PTI Punjab general secretary Chaudhry Bilal Ejaz said five party lawmakers were among 25 others arrested in Lahore.“Despite this era of oppression, repression, and fascism, a large number of PTI workers and office-bearers in Punjab staged protest rallies and pledged to stand with Imran Khan,” he told news agency PTI.According to PTI, at least 50 workers were arrested in Mianwali, Rawalpindi and other parts of Punjab. In Karachi, police used tear gas to disperse PTI supporters protesting in Saddar Town and arrested more than 10 demonstrators. The party also claimed six workers were arrested in Pano Aqil and 15 in Kandhkot.On Wednesday, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa chief minister Muhammad Suhail Afridi announced that PTI supporters will march towards Islamabad on September 27 if 'justice' is not provided to Khan.Addressing supporters in Peshawar, Afridi said the party's first demand was for cases against Khan and his wife to be heard and decided on merit. Its second demand, he said, was restoration of meetings with their legal team, doctors, relatives and party leaders.He claimed that if justice is delivered, Khan can be released “within 30 minutes”. Otherwise, he said, people from across Pakistan will march to Islamabad on September 27.Aleema Khan, sister of the ousted PM, said the movement for his release had already begun and its next phase would be announced soon.PTI senior leader Moonis Elahi alleged that Khan “has been denied meetings and proper medical treatment, and his eyesight has also deteriorated” in prison.Khan, 73, was arrested on August 5, 2023, and has remained in prison while facing multiple cases. His party has repeatedly alleged that the cases are politically motivated, a charge denied by the Shehbaz Sharif-led government.Amnesty International, a global non-governmental organization, also called on Pakistani authorities to uphold Khan's rights. Acting Regional Director for South Asia Isabelle Lassee said, “For three years, Pakistan’s authorities have systematically denied Imran Khan the right to a fair trial, subjected him to prolonged solitary confinement, and limited his access to medical care and visitation rights.”Lassee further said Khan had not been allowed to meet his family for more than eight months and that he and his wife, Bushra Bibi, had been denied regular access to legal counsel since December 2025.
Article Summary: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) supporters held rallies nationwide to mark three years of Imran Khan's imprisonment. The demonstrations, which called for Khan’s release, saw police fire tear gas at protesters in Rawalpindi amid clashes and heightened security. The main rally was held in Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Article Title: Peace talks abroad, protests at home: The many contradictions shaping Pakistan today
Article Text:
Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif and army chief Asim Munir (R) (PTI file photo)

From military confrontation to diplomatic outreach

The Iran gamble

A war next door, and Pakistan's opportunity

Living on lifelines, dreaming of leadership

Source: IMF

Security ambitions amid diplomatic outreach

Diplomacy abroad, discontent within

Operation Sindoor 's lasting fallout

Operation Sindoor fallout

Sites targeted during Op Sindoor

The Balochistan challenge refuses to fade

BLA

Pakistan's uneasy neighbourhood

Presence of TTP remains a major challenge for Pakistan

A nation seeking influence while confronting instability

"A house divided against itself cannot stand." Abraham Lincoln's observation aptly captures Pakistan 's situation.While Islamabad chases the image of an indispensable diplomatic player, its own foundations appear increasingly fragile. From brokering peace in Middle East to courting Washington and Beijing, Pakistan has sought a larger role in global diplomacy.Yet back home, it remains weighed down by economic distress, political unrest, separatist movements, water shortages, terrorism, and accusations of human rights abuses, an uneasy contradiction that defines the country's present-day reality.Much of Pakistan's strategic direction continues to be shaped by its military establishment, with army chief Asim Munir, the country's de facto centre of power. His influence extends well beyond defence matters, as Pakistan's military continues to function as a parallel authority that heavily influences domestic governance as well as foreign policy.That contrast between projecting stability abroad and confronting instability at home, has become one of Pakistan's defining geopolitical challenges.Just over a year ago, Pakistan suffered one of its most difficult periods on the diplomatic and military fronts following India's response to the Pakistan-backed terror attack in South Kashmir's Pahalgam.New Delhi's "zero-tolerance" policy under Prime Minister Narendra Modi translated into a series of retaliatory actions that once again placed Pakistan under international scrutiny over terrorism.Yet, even as tensions with India remained elevated, Islamabad quickly sought to recast its international image.Already maintaining close ties with China, Pakistan simultaneously attempted to deepen engagement with Donald Trump's United States. For a country grappling with a fragile economy, maintaining goodwill with both Washington and Beijing has become increasingly important.It was in this backdrop that Pakistan pitched itself as a potential mediator between Iran and the United States.Pakistan's bid to position itself as a regional peace broker did not begin smoothly.Its initial attempt to host talks between Iran and the United States faltered after Tehran rejected Islamabad as the venue. According to The Wall Street Journal, Iran formally informed mediators that it would not attend the proposed talks with American officials in Pakistan.Islamabad, however, persisted.Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and military head Asim Munir stepped up engagement with Washington, with Munir's growing proximity to the Trump administration earning him the title of Trump's "favourite field marshal".Around the same time, Sharif attended President Xi Jinping 's grand military parade in Beijing alongside leaders including Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.The event reinforced Pakistan's continued strategic closeness with China even as it simultaneously sought stronger engagement with Washington.Six months later, the geopolitical landscape shifted dramatically as President Donald Trump launched military strikes against Iran, joined by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu under Operation Epic Fury.Global Shia icon and longest-ruling Supreme Leader of Iran Ayatollah Ali Khamenei was killed on the opening day of the offensive on February 28, 2026 in Pakistan's neighbourhood.The raging Tehran regime's response left the Middle East region totally disturbed. Bombs, missiles and drones fell, almost hitting every country in the region.Retaliatory strikes and military activity engulfed large parts of the region, with airspace disrupted across Iraq, Kuwait, Syria, Lebanon, Yemen, Oman, Jordan, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.However, Pakistan, despite its border with Iran, remained untouched and safe.That made Islamabad a potential venue for talks with Iran's new leadership under Mojtaba Khamenei .Sensing an opportunity, Pakistan declared itself a peace broker. On April 8, Sharif posted on X announcing a ceasefire that actually wasn't close to peace.He wrote: "With the greatest humility, I am pleased to announce that the Islamic Republic of Iran and the United States of America, along with their allies, have agreed to an immediate ceasefire everywhere including Lebanon and elsewhere, EFFECTIVE IMMEDIATELY."In May, army chief Asim Munir hailed the development as "slight progress". US Vice President JD Vance visited Pakistan twice for peace talks, but despite the diplomatic efforts, the fighting continued and a lasting peace remained elusive.Still, the symbolism was already disheartening. The same country where the US carried out Operation Neptune Spear to eliminate Osama bin Laden had now become Washington's chosen venue for talks with Iran.Islamabad may be eager to wear the badge of a global player, but its economic reality tells a far less flattering story. Beneath the grand diplomatic posturing lies a cash-strapped nation surviving on lifelines from China, the United States, the IMF and other international lenders, hardly the profile of a country calling the shots on the world stage.According to Reuters, the IMF in May completed reviews of its lending programmes with Pakistan, clearing the way for approximately $1.32 billion in fresh funding.The package included nearly $1.1 billion under the Extended Fund Facility and around $220 million under the Resilience and Sustainability Facility, taking total disbursements under the two ongoing programmes to roughly $4.8 billion.Pakistan remains under a $7-billion IMF programme after reaching a staff-level agreement in March."Amid a more challenging and highly uncertain external environment since the onset of the war in the Middle East, Pakistan needs to maintain strong macroeconomic policies while accelerating reform efforts," the IMF said in a statement.For Islamabad, therefore, diplomacy is not merely about regional influence. It is also about preserving the confidence of the international community at a time when its economy remains deeply dependent on external financing.Alongside its mediation efforts, Pakistan has also sought to deepen strategic partnerships within the Islamic world.Islamabad has moved closer to Turkey and Saudi Arabia, readying a Nato-style Islamic security arrangement with mutual defence provisions reminiscent to Nato.The defence pact, signed by Pakistan and Saudi Arabia in September, states that "any aggression" against one member would be treated as an attack on all , a provision that closely mirrors Nato's Article 5. Turkey, already a Nato member, fields the alliance's second-largest military after the United States.While the arrangement remains far from becoming a formal military alliance, it reflects Islamabad's broader effort to strengthen its regional security architecture to counter New Delhi.However, the economic and military size of the two-nuclear armed nations still remain widely different.Pakistan lagging far behind.Even with Islamabad's projected flamboyancy in foreign dealings, unrest continues across Pakistan and regions illegally occupied by Pakistan.The most visible flashpoint in recent months has been Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK), where the so-called Assembly elections have been conducted in three phases amid allegations of police excesses and restrictions on dissent.Videos and reports emerging from the region have shown violent confrontations between security forces and protesters, prompting criticism from rights groups and attracting international attention.Pakistan's own defence minister, Khawaja Asif, further fuelled controversy with remarks defending the government's actions."I put the protesters of PoJK in the same category as India and consider them as enemies," Asif said.The statement reflected Islamabad's increasingly uncompromising approach towards dissent in the region.The ministry of external affairs strongly denounced Pakistan's mischievous handling of the situation, describing the elections in PoK as a "complete farce". The MEA also condemned the Islamabad-backed ill-treatment and crackdown that killed 90 people in the region since June this year.Human rights organisations have echoed similar concerns.Amnesty International USA called reports emerging from PoK's Rawalakot as "disturbing" and urged Pakistani authorities to restore communication services and permit independent media and observers into the region."The disturbing reports emerging from Rawalakot are consistent with the Pakistani authorities' long history of unlawful violence against protesters in PoJK. We urge the Pakistani authorities to restore all communications access and allow media and independent observers into the area," Amnesty International USA posted on X.The developments have reinforced criticism that, while Islamabad attempts to mediate conflicts abroad, it continues to face accusations of suppressing dissent within territories under its own control.Behind the fancy overcoat of its foreign policy ambitions, Pakistan ultimately bore the brunt of its fertile terror fields it had long nurtured.The fallout from Operation Sindoor did not just damage Pakistan-backed terror camps and military infrastructure.India swiftly showcased the scale of its response, striking nine terror bases and 11 military installations across Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK).The consequences of Operation Sindoor extended beyond military targets to the country's most basic necessities, including water. With all major rivers in Pakistan flowing into its territory from India, New Delhi had placed the decades-old Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance immediately after the Pahalgam massacre of April 22, 2025.The country is facing an increasingly severe water crisis, particularly across Sindh and Balochistan , where shrinking river flows and uneven distribution have triggered alarm among farmers, political leaders and water experts.Months after New Delhi's decision, Pakistan is confronting growing concerns over agricultural losses, declining livelihoods and mounting economic pressure across several provinces.Sindh, home to Karachi, Pakistan's financial capital, has emerged as one of the worst-hit regions, with water shortages threatening agriculture and affecting millions of people.Prime Minister Narendra Modi had encapsulated India's position soon after the Pahalgam attack."Terror and talks cannot go together; water and blood cannot flow together," he had said.The message was reiterated recently by defence minister Rajnath Singh recently on Kargil Vijay Diwas."After the Pahalgam terror attack, by suspending the Indus Waters Treaty, we said that those whose tears have dried up should not expect water from us. We will not let the waters of the Sindhu reach the patrons of terrorists and enemies of humanity," Rajnath said.For Pakistan, the water crisis has added yet another layer to an already fragile economic and political situation, with experts warning that prolonged shortages could further aggravate regional discontent.While PoK has dominated headlines in recent weeks, Balochistan continues to represent Pakistan's longest-running internal security challenge.The province recently announced plans to observe its own Independence Day, underlining the persistence of separatist sentiment.The conflict, rooted in grievances dating back to Balochistan's accession to Pakistan in 1948, revolves around demands for greater political autonomy, control over natural resources and opposition to mega infrastructure projects such as the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC).Over the decades, the conflict has been marked by armed insurgency, heavy militarisation and repeated allegations of human rights violations.Yet Balochistan is only one strand of Pakistan's broader internal unrest.The country's dissent is neither unified nor driven by a single cause.Separatist groups in Balochistan, the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, political activists and unemployed youth often pursue vastly different objectives.That fragmentation, however, has also worked to the advantage of Pakistan's establishment.Without a unified opposition, the state has been able to confront each movement differently, labelling one as terrorism, another as separatism, others as political disorder or foreign conspiracy.Rather than confronting a single nationwide challenge, Islamabad faces multiple disconnected crises, each requiring a different response.For neighbouring Iran, Pakistan has recently struck the chord of "peace", offering itself as a mediator, though the negotiations have yielded almost no progress.Its ties with Tehran, however, have rarely been straightforward. Relations with India remain frozen, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi making New Delhi's position unequivocal: "If there will be talks between India and Pakistan, it will only be on terrorism and PoK."To the west, Pakistan's troubles are no less daunting. Crossborder tensions with Taliban-ruled Afghanistan have intensified, even as Islamabad grapples with a surge in terror attacks at home.Beyond the long-running insurgency in Balochistan, Pakistan faces an increasingly potent threat from the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). While the Afghan Taliban returned to power in 2021, Islamabad's hopes of gaining strategic leverage quickly unraveled. Kabul has refused to dismantle TTP sanctuaries, allowing the outfit to regroup and intensify attacks across Pakistan.The fallout has been severe. Cross-border clashes have become more frequent, while the TTP, an umbrella militant group formed in 2007, continues to challenge the Pakistani state's authority, specifying the irony of a country seeking to broker peace abroad while battling an escalating insurgency at home.Pakistan today finds itself pursuing two parallel realities.On one hand, it is attempting to establish itself as a regional diplomatic player, offering to mediate conflicts, expanding defence partnerships and seeking greater geopolitical relevance.On the other, it continues to wrestle with economic fragility, dependence on IMF assistance, unrest in PoK and Balochistan, a worsening water crisis and an increasingly complex internal security landscape.Adding to these challenges is the country's continued struggle with terrorism. According to the Global Terrorism Index 2026, Pakistan ranked as the country most affected by terrorism, recording more than 1,000 terror-related deaths in 2025, its worst figures since 2013.For Islamabad, diplomatic visibility on the global stage may offer strategic dividends and international goodwill. But as long as domestic crises continue to deepen, Pakistan's ambitions abroad will remain overshadowed by the challenges it faces at home.
Article Summary: Pakistan has sought a larger role in global diplomacy. But back home, it remains weighed down by economic distress, political unrest, separatist movements, terrorism, and accusations of human rights abuses. The contrast between projecting stability abroad and confronting instability at home, has become one of Pakistan's defining geopolitical challenges.

Article Title: 'Long history of unlawful violence': Global watchdogs condemn Pakistan's crackdown in PoK
Article Text:
PoK (File photo)

As Pakistan-occupied Kashmir goes through its so-called assembly polls, reports of brutality, violence and unrest continue to surface, with global human rights and press freedom watchdogs raising alarm over an escalating crackdown on protesters and the media.International organisations, including Amnesty International and the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), have flagged allegations of state-backed violence, restrictions on independent reporting, enforced disappearances of journalists and prolonged internet shutdowns. They have urged Pakistani authorities to end the crackdown, restore communication services and ensure transparent investigations into alleged human rights violations.Highlighting reports of excessive force used against demonstrators in Rawalakot, Amnesty International said the incidents reflected Pakistan's long record of using unlawful violence against protesters."The disturbing reports emerging from Rawalakot are consistent with the Pakistani authorities' long history of unlawful violence against protesters. A prompt, independent, and transparent investigation must be ordered into the security forces' use of force against protesters.So long as an internet and mobile services blackout remains in place, it will severely impede the independent verification of the full extent of the situation on the ground. We urge the Pakistani authorities to restore all communications access and allow media and independent observers into the area," Amnesty said in a post on X.Echoing similar concerns, CPJ said it was monitoring the deteriorating press freedom situation in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, citing internet blackouts, telecommunications shutdowns, reporting restrictions and the detention and disappearance of journalists.The press freedom watchdog also expressed concern over the reported disappearance of independent journalist Razi Tahir and his colleague Muhammad Saif, who were allegedly taken by men in police uniforms from their office in Islamabad on August 1."CPJ is deeply concerned by reports that independent journalist Razi Tahir and his colleague Muhammad Saif have been missing since August 1. They were reportedly taken by men in police uniforms from their office in Islamabad, and their whereabouts remain unknown. Pakistani authorities must acknowledge whether they are in state custody, ensure due process, and immediately release them if they are being arbitrarily detained," it wrote.In a subsequent update, CPJ said the two journalists remain missing while Kashmiri journalist Raja Ikram, who was reportedly detained in Islamabad on August 1, has since been released."Journalists Razi Tahir and Muhmmad Saif remain missing after reportedly being taken by men in police uniform on August 1. Pakistani authorities must acknowledge their detention if they are in state custody, ensure due process, and immediately release them. Kashmiri journalist Raja Ikram, who was reportedly detained in Islamabad on August 1, was later released," it added.CPJ also said the media crackdown appears to be extending beyond the region, pointing to reported action against major news outlets alongside continuing telecommunications disruptions.The criticism comes as casualties continue to mount during the ongoing protest movement. According to figures released by the Human Rights Council of Pakistan-occupied Jammu & Kashmir (HRC-PoJK) as of Sunday, at least 80 people have died, including 33 civilians before July 27, 43 people killed since July 27 across Rawalakot, Mirpur and Muzaffarabad, and four Pakistan-occupied Jammu & Kashmir police personnel.
Article Summary: Watchdogs raise alarm over escalating crackdown on protesters and the media. Amnesty International, Committee to Protect Journalists have flagged allegations of state-backed violence, restrictions on independent reporting and enforced disappearances of journalists. They have urged Pakistani authorities to end the crackdown, restore communication services and ensure transparent investigations.

Article Title: 'They'll arrest us at hospitals': PoK protesters risk death over electricity, flour demands
Article Text:
Dozens killed in PoK as protesters treating gunshot wounds in makeshift clinics avoid hospitals for fear of arrest

Makeshift clinic treats dozens of critically injured

JAAC and authorities trade accusations

Food shortages, roadblocks add to tensions

A protest movement in PoK has escalated into deadly clashes between security forces and demonstrators, with dozens of people reportedly killed across the region in recent weeks, the BBC reported.The protests have been led by the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), which has been demanding cheaper electricity and flour as well as better access to education, healthcare and other basic services. The movement says an agreement reached with the governments of Pakistan and PoK in October to address some of its demands has not been implemented.The BBC reported that Rawalakot, one of the main centres of the protests, was experiencing severe disruption, with roads blocked, shops shut and internet access cut off.The BBC visited a makeshift clinic near the main protest site, where a spare bedroom had been converted into a medical supply area and a bed placed outside beneath a tarpaulin was being used to treat injured protesters.A doctor identified by the BBC as Dr Anwar said the clinic had treated around 50 to 60 critically injured people since July 27, including an estimated 15 to 20 people with gunshot wounds.The doctor said the facility could provide basic emergency treatment, including stopping bleeding, dressing wounds and removing superficial bullets, but lacked the equipment required for serious injuries involving the chest, abdomen, head or other vital organs.He also said protesters were reluctant to seek treatment at the main hospital because of fears they could be arrested or shot there. Authorities have rejected that claim.The BBC spoke to families who said relatives had been shot during the protests. One woman, identified as Asma, said she was at a demonstration when she learned that her only son had been shot. Another man, Salman, told the BBC that his younger brother had died.The JAAC says its demonstrations are peaceful and focused on economic and basic-rights demands. The group has rejected allegations that it is responsible for violence, while authorities have accused it of being armed and attempting to disrupt ongoing elections in the region.The JAAC was banned in June and labelled foreign-funded terrorists by the authorities, according to the BBC. The group rejected the characterisation and said its financial support was from the PoK diaspora and not India, an accusation that Pakistan has tried to make on multiple occasions.Authorities have also accused the group of attacking law-enforcement personnel and obstructing public order. Officials have released drone footage that they said showed JAAC members carrying guns on rooftops and displayed weapons they said had been recovered from the group.The government has rejected allegations that security forces fired indiscriminately at peaceful protesters, saying law-enforcement personnel acted against people involved in attacks on security forces, threats to public safety or obstruction of lawful authority.The JAAC, meanwhile, has alleged that security forces were responsible for firing on protesters. Umar Nazir, a member of the group's core committee, also alleged that people had infiltrated the movement and may have carried out violence to support the authorities' narrative, though he provided no evidence for the claim.The BBC said that during protests it attended, its journalists saw no weapons or shooting among demonstrators, although gunshots were heard overnight and it could not establish who was firing or at what.The unrest has also disrupted supplies in Rawalakot. The BBC reported seeing food shortages, with most shops closed and protesters sharing available food. Some residents described attempts to smuggle rice into the city.Several roads have been blocked by fallen trees and other debris. Authorities have blamed the JAAC for the blockades, while also denying that they were preventing food or medical supplies from reaching Rawalakot.The protests come as local elections are taking place in PoK, adding another layer of tension to the confrontation.
Article Summary: Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) has been demanding cheaper electricity and flour as well as better access to education, healthcare and other basic services. The BBC visited a makeshift clinic near the main protest site, where a spare bedroom had been converted into a medical supply area. A doctor said the clinic had treated around 50 to 60 critically injured people since July 27.

Article Title: '15-year-olds shot, only asked for basic rights': Inside the deadly PoK crackdown
Article Text:
Deadly clashes continue during protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir

'Most victims were 15 to 35'

'We are not terrorists'

Teenagers as young as 15 have been among those killed or seriously injured in a sweeping crackdown on protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK), according to a report by the BBC based on the accounts of residents, doctors and families from the protest hub of Rawalakot. The demonstrations in Rawalakot by the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) have turned deadly amid an ongoing security operation.The report said that dozens of people have been killed across the region over the past two months in clashes between security forces and protesters. The demonstrations comes as local elections are underway in the region.A doctor identified as Dr Anwar said that he had treated 50 to 60 critically injured patients since July 27, including 15 to 20 people with gunshot wounds."Most of those who have been killed or seriously injured are young people between about 15-16 years old and 32-35 years old. I have seen very few patients over the age of 40," BBC quoted the doctor saying.According to the report, many injured protesters have avoided government hospitals fearing arrest or being shot, a claim denied by the authorities.Families of those killed described the protests as a movement for basic rights, including affordable electricity, flour, education and healthcare."We only asked for affordable flour, electricity and our basic rights," Ali, whose friend Shafqat Hussain was fatally shot, told the BBC. "Instead, our brothers are being killed. What was our crime? Why are live bullets being fired at us?"Asma, whose only son was killed, said: "We were only asking for our rights. We are not terrorists." She added, "He knew there were risks, but he believed standing up for justice was important. He used to say that dying for a just cause was an honour."Another resident, Salman, whose younger brother died during the protests, told the BBC: "He was the youngest in the family and was loved by everyone... I feel proud that he gave his life while standing up for the rights of the people. He was not fighting or attacking anyone."The JAAC says the protests stem from the government's failure to implement an agreement signed in October that promised relief on electricity prices and other public welfare issues.The group, which was banned in June and designated by authorities as a foreign-funded terrorist organisation, denies the allegation, insisting it is a peaceful movement funded by the PoK diaspora.The Pakistan-occupied Kashmir government has rejected allegations that security forces fired indiscriminately at peaceful protesters. It said law enforcement acted only against individuals involved in attacks on security personnel, threats to public safety or obstruction of lawful authority.
Article Summary: Dozens of people have been killed across the region over the past two months in clashes between security forces and protesters. The demonstrations in Rawalakot by the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) have turned deadly amid an ongoing security operation. The Pakistan-occupied Kashmir government has rejected allegations that security forces fired indiscriminately at peaceful protesters.

Article Title: 'Do not befriend Kaafirs': Pakistani general levels terror allegations against India
Article Text:
Pakistan's military spokesperson Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry

Pakistan's military spokesperson, Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, has sparked controversy after saying in a video that Muslims should not befriend "kaafirs" (non-believers), warning that those who do would no longer be considered among the faithful."Do not befriend kaafirs (non-believers) and leave the faithful. If you do that, there's a problem. Then you are not among the Muslims," Chaudhry said while addressing a press conference.“Now our population is 240-250 million people, and we still have four provinces. We have to see whether this is serving the purpose of good governance. That debate has to be sensibly held by politicians, by those in power, even those who have previously been in power, and those who are responsible to the people of Pakistan,” he added.The remarks were made during a wider media briefing that focused on Pakistan's counter-terrorism operations, the security situation in Balochistan, and the country's ties with Afghanistan.Taking a jibe at India-Afghanistan ties, Chaudhry claimed that the Afghan Taliban regime's "business" was terrorism, alleging that it used militancy to sustain its economy, state institutions and diplomacy.“Even their diplomacy is centred on terrorism. What is common between India and Afghanistan, except their DNA? The only thing common is terrorism,” Chaudhary said, as cited by Dawn.Chaudhry also claimed that around 300 Indian websites were being used to support terrorism-related activities in Balochistan, while more than 1,000 social media accounts and what he described as a "hostile diaspora" were involved in spreading propaganda linked to terrorism.“First, an event or incident is seeded, right or wrong, and then it is framed by initiators, who hand it over to amplifiers. Then mass amplification is done by mainstream Indian media, channels and their print media as well, from where it is picked up by international media, and then you take it and run it as facts," he said.The DG ISPR said the government was also working to strengthen the police force, including by deploying newly recruited assistant superintendents of police (ASPs) to Balochistan and providing bulletproof vehicles, among other measures.The remarks come amid a series of attacks on Pakistani security forces across Balochistan last month, with armed clashes also reported during military operations in the Mastung and Kech districts, according to The Balochistan Post (TBP).The insurgency in Balochistan has been led by several separatist groups, including the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA), which has waged a long-running campaign against Pakistan's federal government. The group has frequently targeted security personnel and infrastructure in the province and has also carried out attacks in other parts of the country, including Karachi.According to Pakistan's 2023 census, Balochistan is home to around 15 million people and is rich in natural resources, including coal, gold, copper and natural gas. The BLA maintains that these resources should belong to the people of Balochistan and opposes the federal government's control over their extraction and the province's security.
Article Summary: Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said Muslims should not befriend "kaafirs" (non-believers) He warned that those who do would no longer be considered among the faithful. The remarks were made during a wider media briefing on Pakistan's counter-terrorism operations.

Article Title: Pakistan restricts digital news websites reporting on PoK protests, crackdowns: Report
Article Text:
Pakistan expands online curbs following coverage of PoK unrest

Pakistan has reportedly expanded digital censorship measures by restricting access to several news websites following extensive media coverage of the ongoing unrest in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK).Alongside the reported blocking of local and regional news websites, international broadcasters, have also become inaccessible to users in parts of Pakistan, according to media reports cited by ANI.The restrictions appear to target platforms covering the recent protests, alleged security crackdowns and growing public discontent in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK). Pakistani authorities have not officially confirmed the reported restrictions.The channels facing possible blocking include those linked to Pakistan's main opposition party, its leader and jailed former prime minister Imran Khan, as well as several journalists critical of the government, according to a court order dated June 24.Earlier in July, Al Jazeera reported that a judicial magistrate's court in Islamabad had ordered the blocking of several YouTube channels based on a June 2 report by Pakistan's National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA).The agency alleged that the channels had published content that was "intimidating", "provocative" and "derogatory" towards state institutions and public officials.Al Jazeera reported that digital rights groups have warned the proposed bans could further restrict freedom of expression in Pakistan. With television and print media facing significant curbs, social media remains one of the few platforms for public debate and dissent, the report said.The broadcaster also reported that YouTube had notified 27 content creators that their channels could be blocked if they failed to comply with the court's directives.The restrictions come amid heightened sensitivity over the flow of information related to the political situation and local protests in PoK.The second phase of elections in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK) was marred by widespread disruptions, logistical challenges and continuing protests, raising fresh concerns over the credibility of the electoral process.Polling was held across 21 constituencies, including nine in the Muzaffarabad Division of PoK and 12 refugee constituencies located in different parts of Pakistan.Voting was disrupted in several constituencies as road blockades and protests affected access to polling stations and delayed the electoral process.
Article Summary: Pakistani authorities have not officially confirmed the reported restrictions. The restrictions appear to target platforms covering the recent protests, alleged security crackdowns and growing public discontent in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK) Earlier in July, a judicial magistrate's court in Islamabad ordered the blocking of several YouTube channels.

Article Title: 'Double tap': How terrorists are trapping Pakistan's security personnel
Article Text:
The latest assault came on Sunday, when a suicide bomber struck outside a police station in Swat's Kabal town during an anti-terror rally

A 'double tap' strategy to maximise casualties

Recent attacks expose worsening security crisis

Pakistan's security forces are increasingly facing a deadly challenge as militant groups adopt a "double tap" strategy that turns rescue missions into ambushes. The tactic, analysed by Pakistani newspaper Dawn, involves an initial attack on a police or security installation, followed by a second strike targeting reinforcements rushing to the scene.The evolving strategy has coincided with a sharp rise in militant violence, particularly in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where police and military personnel have repeatedly come under attack in recent months. The latest assault came on Sunday, when a suicide bomber struck outside a police station in Swat's Kabal town during an anti-terror rally, killing at least 14 people, including police personnel, and injuring 18 others.According to an analysis by Dawn, militants have refined their tactics by carrying out coordinated two-stage attacks aimed at inflicting the highest possible casualties on responding security forces.The first team attacks a police station, checkpost or security installation, drawing personnel into a firefight. Simultaneously, another militant group positions itself along likely reinforcement routes.As additional police or military teams rush to assist, they are targeted through improvised explosive devices (IEDs), roadside ambushes or quadcopters capable of dropping explosives.Dawn said predictable response patterns have repeatedly turned reinforcement teams into easy targets. Over the past three years, at least 16 police personnel, including three deputy superintendents of police (DSPs), have been killed while responding to attacks rather than during the initial assault.The newspaper pointed to the July 29 attack in Hangu district as the latest example. Terrorists first stormed a police checkpost before attacking the reinforcements sent to support officers already under fire. Nine police personnel, including DSP Diyar Khan, were killed and 28 others injured. According to Dawn, it was the third major incident in which the second phase of the attack caused the heaviest losses.The pattern dates back to January 2023, when DSP Sardar Hussain and two of his guards were killed in an IED blast while responding to an attack on the Sarband police station near Peshawar.The strategy has unfolded alongside a broader escalation in militant attacks across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.On July 24, at least 15 people, including 14 security personnel, were killed after Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) militants attacked a joint police checkpost in Tank district. According to Pakistan's military, the attackers first attempted to breach the facility but were repelled before ramming an explosives-laden vehicle into the perimeter wall, triggering a massive blast that destroyed much of the checkpost. Security forces said 15 militants were killed during the operation, while 12 soldiers, two policemen and a forest department official lost their lives.Sunday's suicide bombing in Swat further highlighted the deteriorating security environment. The attacker detonated explosives after police attempted to stop and search him outside the Kabal police station, according to Dawn. The blast occurred near a large public demonstration where residents had gathered to protest the resurgence of militancy and demand stronger state action.Speakers at the rally criticised authorities for failing to curb militant activity and urged the government to restore lasting peace in the valley, which was once cleared of insurgents after a major military operation but has seen renewed militant activity in recent months.Data cited by Dawn from the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies showed that Khyber Pakhtunkhwa recorded 154 terrorism-related deaths in July, more than double the 75 fatalities reported in June, underscoring the rapidly worsening security situation.
Article Summary: Pakistan's security forces are increasingly facing a deadly challenge. Militants adopt a 'double tap' strategy that turns rescue missions into ambushes. The tactic involves an initial attack on a police or security installation, followed by a second strike targeting reinforcements rushing to the scene.

Article Title: Peace rally in Pakistan rocked by suicide blast; 14 killed, 20 injured
Article Text:
The blast occurred near Kabal Chowk, where residents had assembled for the 'Olasi Pasoon' peace gathering

PTM condemns attack on peace gathering

Death toll rises as investigation begins

Attack shakes peace rally

Rising militant violence in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa

Pakistani leaders condemn bombing
